name: Command Dashboard (Analytics)
route: Log in at http://localhost:8080 as admin@city.gov / admin123 — staff land on the Dashboard automatically. Otherwise click "Dashboard" (first item) in the top nav.
one_liner: One auto-refreshing command view that reconciles 2,001 citizen complaints, the whole case pipeline, citizen satisfaction ratings and the LIVE VisionScan vector index into ten KPI tiles and six charts, with no charting library and no network dependency.

headline.what: Ten KPI tiles that reconcile two different systems on one row — the CityShield case database AND the running VisionScan FAISS index. "INDEXED FRAMES 417" is read from the live index object (get_clip_index().ntotal), not from a table.
headline.why_impressive: A judge expects a dashboard to be SELECT COUNT(*) over one DB. This one proves the AI search index and the policing case system are the same product: 16 camera feeds, 417 CLIP-embedded frames, 2,001 complaints, 10 cases, all in one header. I verified every tile against /api/analytics/summary and they matched exactly, digit for digit.
headline.exact_steps: Log in as admin@city.gov / admin123. The dashboard is the landing page. Read across the top row, then drop to the second row and point at FEEDS 16 / INDEXED FRAMES 417 and say "those two come from the live vector index, not the database."

headline.what: The 14-day complaints trend — 14 bars, every single one populated, hover gives the exact date and count.
headline.why_impressive: Dense, gap-filled series with no holes: I read the title attribute off all 14 bars and none was zero (16,14,14,16,11,10,14,9,8,11,16,8,12,7 = 166 complaints in 14 days). The backend fills missing days with 0 rather than dropping them, so the axis never lies about a quiet day.
headline.exact_steps: Hover the rightmost bar — the native tooltip reads "2026-08-19: 7". Hover the tallest (leftmost or 08-16) — "2026-08-06: 16".

headline.what: Closed-loop service metrics: AVG RESOLVE 115h and AVG RATING 4.2/5 (5) sitting next to OPEN CASES / CLOSED.
headline.why_impressive: Most hackathon dashboards show inputs (complaints filed). This shows OUTCOMES — how long a case actually took to close, computed as AVG((julianday(closed_at)-julianday(created_at))*24) over closed cases, and what the citizen scored it afterwards. It is the citizen-portal loop closing in a number.
headline.exact_steps: Point at the AVG RESOLVE and AVG RATING tiles together and say "complaint in, case out, citizen rates it, and that rating is on this screen."

headline.what: Six breakdown widgets — cases-by-status donut, complaints-by-category, complaints-by-status, cases-by-severity, top complaint locations — all hand-rolled SVG/CSS with zero charting dependency.
headline.why_impressive: No Chart.js, no Recharts, no CDN. The whole dashboard renders offline in an air-gapped police network, which is exactly the deployment constraint a government buyer cares about. The donut is a single <svg> with stroke-dasharray arcs.
headline.exact_steps: If asked about the stack: "frontend/src/components/platform/charts.jsx — 104 lines, three primitives, no chart library, so it works with the network cable pulled."

headline.what: It is genuinely live — measured, not claimed.
headline.why_impressive: The header says "live · refreshes every 15s". I counted the outbound /api/analytics/summary calls: exactly one extra in a 17-second window. If someone converts a complaint to a case in another tab, this screen catches it within 15s.
headline.exact_steps: Say it, don't wait for it on stage. (If you want to demo it: have a second person close a case, then watch CLOSED tick up within 15s.)

questions.q: Is "417 indexed frames" a database row count or the actual search index?
questions.a: The actual index. analytics.py imports get_clip_index() and reads .ntotal off the running FAISS object — it is the only KPI on this page that does not come from SQLite. It happens to equal COUNT(*) FROM frames (417) right now, which is the correct invariant: every extracted keyframe got embedded.

questions.q: 2,001 complaints — is that real Ahmedabad crime data?
questions.a: No, and we say so on the City Map footer and in docs/AHMEDABAD_CRIME_DATA.md. It is a deterministic synthetic 180-day stream generated from public NCRB/press-derived area profiles (seed_synthetic.py, fixed RNG seed). The 9 cases, 30 evidence items and 5 ratings on this screen are real actions taken through the real UI.

questions.q: How is "avg resolve 115h" computed?
questions.a: AVG((julianday(closed_at) - julianday(created_at)) * 24.0) over cases WHERE status='closed' AND closed_at IS NOT NULL. Cases still open contribute nothing, so it is a survivor-biased number by construction — it answers "how long did the ones we finished take", not "how long does a case take".

questions.q: Open 4 + closed 6 = 10 cases, but 2,001 complaints. Where did the other 1,991 go?
questions.a: Complaints and cases are different entities. A complaint is a citizen report; it becomes a case only when an officer triages and converts it. The complaints-by-status chart shows exactly 9 in state 'converted' — those are the ones that became cases. The other 1,992 sit in submitted (809) / under_review (799) / assigned (384). That ratio is deliberate: it is what a real station backlog looks like.

questions.q: What charting library is this?
questions.a: None. charts.jsx is 104 lines of hand-written SVG and CSS — three primitives (BarList, Donut, TrendBars). No Chart.js, no Recharts, no CDN font or script. The whole page renders with the network cable pulled, which matters for a police intranet deployment.

questions.q: How live is "live"?
questions.a: 15-second poll of /api/analytics/summary — I measured exactly one extra request in a 17-second window. It is polling, not websockets; that is a deliberate choice because the numbers are aggregates that change on the order of minutes, and polling survives a proxy that kills long-lived connections.

questions.q: Why does the users tile say 5 when you seed 4 accounts?
questions.a: Because someone registered a citizen account through the public register form during testing — the tile is genuinely live. The four seeded accounts are admin@city.gov, lead@city.gov, officer@city.gov and citizen@example.com.

questions.q: Can I filter this by date range or station?
questions.a: Not on this screen — honestly, no. The window is a fixed 14 days and /api/analytics/summary takes no parameters. The date/category filtering lives on the City Map (Reports layer), which has category and 7/30/90/all-time selectors.

questions.q: What happens if the backend is slow or down?
questions.a: The page shows a spinner until the first response, then an error box on failure, and retries every 15s. The failure mode I actually hit was a 429 from the per-IP rate limiter, which blanks the whole dashboard to "Too many requests" until the next poll. That is a real weakness — the error branch is all-or-nothing rather than keeping the last good render.

broken: TOMORROW MORNING THE LAST BAR WILL BE ZERO. Verified, not guessed: I replayed the backend's exact dense-fill query against the live DB with 'now' set to 2026-08-20 04:00 UTC (~09:30 IST) and got Aug 07..Aug 19 with real values and 2026-08-20 = 0. Cause: the chart window uses SQLite date('now'), which is UTC and rolls over at 05:30 IST, while the synthetic complaint stream is a ONE-SHOT marker-gated insert whose newest row is 2026-08-19 16:46:52 UTC. The seed does not roll forward. So the fix you made today is correct for today only. Options before the demo: (a) accept it — it is one 1px stub at the right edge of 14 bars and nobody will notice; (b) shift the newest complaints forward by one day; (c) re-seed. Do NOT run seed with force — it INSERTs again without clearing and would double the stream to ~4,000 complaints.

KPI DRIFT — the numbers in your brief are already stale. Measured at 00:52: closed 5, avg resolve 138h, evidence 28, total cases 9, users 4. Measured at 01:20 the same night: closed 6, avg resolve 115h, evidence 30, total cases 10, users 5. Complaints (2001), feeds (16) and indexed frames (417) did NOT move. This is concurrent testing writing to the demo DB, not a bug — but re-read the tiles on the morning and do not read numbers off a script.

A SINGLE 429 BLANKS THE ENTIRE DASHBOARD. AnalyticsView's error branch replaces every tile and chart with one red "Too many requests" box. I hit this repeatedly. Root cause worth knowing: the limiter is 120 req/min keyed on request.client.host, and because nginx proxies /api the backend sees the nginx container IP for EVERY browser — so all browsers share ONE bucket. One idle tab already burns 70 req/min (measured). Two tabs open on this stack ≈ 140/min and everything starts 429-ing. On stage: keep exactly one tab open, and close any other machine pointed at the app.

name: City Map (Ahmedabad GIS + predictive forecast + patrol routing)
route: Log in as admin@city.gov / admin123, then click "City Map" in the top nav (4th item). Allow ~10s for the first render — it fires four API calls plus the OSM tile layer.
one_liner: An Ahmedabad crime-intelligence map with three switchable data layers, a glass-box recency-weighted risk forecast whose every point is decomposed back to its source category, a rolling-origin backtest panel with baselines and an oracle ceiling, and a 2-opt patrol router that turns the forecast into physical routes from Cyber Crime Branch HQ.

headline.what: Click any circle on the Risk forecast layer and the popup does not just give a score — it decomposes it. Bapunagar reads "Risk 100 = prior 4 + 48 from recent assault (+2 more) over 215 reports (recency-decayed)" with a stacked bar whose segments sum exactly to the displayed score.
headline.why_impressive: This is the single strongest answer to "predictive policing is a black box". Every point of the 0-100 score is attributable to a named term — the static prior, each crime category's recency-decayed contribution, and the live anomaly boost. The normalisation is affine and the -min offset is folded into the prior specifically so the bar adds up. An officer can audit why a locality got flagged; a judge can too.
headline.exact_steps: Layer toggle -> "Risk forecast". Click the biggest red circle (Bapunagar, north-east of centre). Read the "Why this hotspot?" line out loud. Then click the ⓘ next to "Top predicted hotspots" in the right panel to show the model card with every published coefficient.

headline.what: The "Model accuracy (backtested)" panel — real out-of-sample numbers, four ranking strategies side by side, and an oracle ceiling that makes the headline honest.
headline.why_impressive: Hit-Rate@10 0.78, PAI@10 2.35x against a perfect-hindsight ceiling of 2.53x = 93% of what is achievable on this data, with a 90% bootstrap CI of [0.76, 0.81] over 8 weekly rolling-origin folds. Under it, the baseline table: model 2.35x, frequency 2.22x, prior-only 1.95x, random 1.05x. Almost nobody at a hackathon puts a chance floor and a ceiling next to their own number. And the panel prints its own disclaimer that the data is synthetic.
headline.exact_steps: Right-hand panel, top card. Click "Model accuracy (backtested)" to expand. It is already cached server-side (~10 min TTL) so it opens instantly — I measured the API at 0.25s warm.

headline.what: "Caught 3/3 planted crime waves" — surge detection. "Maninagar surfaced rank 5→3 the week its chain snatching wave hit."
headline.why_impressive: This is the cleanest evidence the model reacts to emerging hotspots instead of parroting a static prior. Time-boxed surges were planted in the seed; the harness scores the model at the surge's end and against the counterfactual just before it began, and reports the rank jump. Maninagar 5→3, SG Highway 6→4, Satellite 10→9, all three inside the top-10 while their surge was live.
headline.exact_steps: It is the first, green-highlighted block inside the expanded accuracy panel. Read the Maninagar line verbatim.

headline.what: Patrol routing: press one button and the forecast becomes physical routes. 2 units, 12 hotspots, dashed polylines drawn from Cyber Crime Branch HQ (Shahibaug) — Unit 1 28.8 km / ~69 min, Unit 2 33.3 km / ~80 min.
headline.why_impressive: It closes the loop from analytics to action, and the routing is real: balanced greedy assignment by centroid proximity with a ceil(n/units) fairness cap, then nearest-neighbour seeding, then 2-opt polish, all on haversine distances. Pure stdlib — no Google Directions, no external routing API, so it runs offline. Measured latency 0.05 seconds.
headline.exact_steps: Set the unit dropdown (top-right) to "2 units", click "Plan patrol routes". Two dashed coloured polylines appear over the map and a "Patrol plan" card lists each unit's ordered stops with km and ETA. Then click "Export CSV" on that card.

headline.what: The Cyber fraud layer with a deliberate, defensible framing: "₹2.1 Cr lost citywide · 164 victims · last 90 days" and the subtitle "Victim-location density — where victims live, not where fraudsters operate."
headline.why_impressive: For a Cyber Crime Branch this is the layer that matters, and the subtitle is the kind of methodological honesty that wins credibility — it names the limitation of the data before anyone else can. Circles are log-scaled by rupees lost, in a distinct violet palette so it never reads as the amber/red crime-density map.

questions.q: What exactly does the forecast predict, and for when?
questions.a: One 7-day window ahead, per locality, on the same 0-100 scale as the current score. predicted_score = current_score × min(growth, 2.0), capped at 100, where growth = (load in the last 7 days + 1) / (load in the 7 days before that + 1). The +1 smoothing stops empty windows exploding and the ×2 cap stops one quiet fortnight producing a nonsense number. Concretely on screen right now: SG Highway 64.9 → 87.0 rising, Bapunagar 100 → 34.9 falling, Vatva 90.8 → 84.5 stable. Across all 30 areas: 9 rising, 9 stable, 12 falling.

questions.q: How do you know it predicts anything? Show me the validation.
questions.a: Rolling-origin (walk-forward) temporal cross-validation, 8 weekly folds over 30 localities, first fold starting 2026-06-24 and the last 2026-08-12. For each fold we score the model with an as_of cutoff so it sees ONLY complaints strictly before the fold start, then grade it against what actually happened in the following 7 days. No future data ever reaches a prediction. Current live numbers: Hit-Rate@10 0.7818, PAI@10 2.345x, Hit-Rate@5 0.5382, PAI@5 3.229x.

questions.q: What is PAI and why should I care about 2.35x?
questions.a: Predictive Accuracy Index, the field standard from Chainey, Tompson & Uhlig (2008): hit-rate divided by the share of the area you are policing. PAI@10 = (crime captured in the top 10 areas / total crime) ÷ (10/30). PAI = 1 is exactly chance — you get 33% of the crime by covering 33% of the city. 2.345 means we concentrate 2.3x more crime per unit of patrol area than blind coverage. Our random baseline measured 1.053x, which is the sanity check that the metric is wired up correctly.

questions.q: 2.35x doesn't sound like much. Is that good?
questions.a: That is the right question, and it is why we publish the oracle ceiling. If you rank each fold by its OWN realised next-week counts — perfect hindsight, the best any predictor could possibly do — PAI@10 is only 2.529x on this data. So 2.345 is 93% of the theoretical maximum. The ceiling is low because the synthetic stream is fairly stationary and lightly contrasted; on lumpier real data both numbers would rise. The honest claim is the percentage of the ceiling, not the absolute.

questions.q: What are the confidence intervals and how were they computed?
questions.a: 90% intervals by bootstrapping over folds: resample the 8 per-fold metrics with replacement 1,000 times, take the 5th and 95th percentiles of the resampled means, fixed seed 20240601 so it reproduces exactly. Hit-Rate@10 [0.757, 0.809]; PAI@10 [2.271, 2.428]; Hit-Rate@5 [0.499, 0.577]. Pure stdlib random/math — no numpy, no sklearn, so it runs anywhere the backend does.

questions.q: What do you compare against? Isn't a naive count just as good?
questions.a: That is nearly true and we publish it rather than hide it. Four strategies on identical folds, PAI@10: model 2.345x, raw all-time frequency 2.220x, static prior-only 1.953x, random 1.053x. So the full model beats a naive complaint count by about 5%. Worse — and this is in our ablation doc — the stripped-down floor actually BEATS the full model at k=5 (Hit-Rate 0.552 vs 0.540). Our advantage exists at k=10 and vanishes at k=5. The headline HR@10 hides that, and I would rather say it than have you find it.

questions.q: Your model has a prior, severity weights, category weights, recency decay, an anomaly boost and a trend term. Which of those actually do anything?
questions.a: Only recency decay, and we measured it. A component ablation (backend/scripts/ablation.py --folds 8, which regenerates docs/ABLATION.md so the doc cannot drift from the code) gives paired ΔHit-Rate@10 with bootstrap CIs: removing recency decay costs -0.045 [-0.068, -0.027] — the only statistically distinguishable term. Static prior +0.012 [0.000, +0.026] and category weighting +0.006 [-0.015, +0.027] point the WRONG way (removing them slightly raised HR@10) but do not clear significance, so we quote them as a direction, never as proven harm. Severity weighting -0.005 [-0.020, +0.005], indistinguishable.

questions.q: And the anomaly boost? It's in your formula and on your model card.
questions.a: It contributes EXACTLY ZERO to the backtest — 0.000, by construction, not by measurement noise. compute_risk() applies the anomaly boost only when as_of is None, and every validation fold passes an as_of, so the term is never evaluated during scoring. That exclusion is deliberate and correct: anomaly events reflect NOW and have no historical timeline, so feeding present-time anomalies into a historical fold would be straight temporal leakage. The honest framing is 'deliberately excluded to avoid leakage', not 'it improves accuracy'. Same for the trend term: TREND_WINDOW_DAYS shapes predicted_score, but compute_risk ranks folds on risk_score, so trend is 0.000 in the backtest too. The README's criteria table was corrected specifically for this.

questions.q: So if the anomaly boost does nothing, why is it in the model at all?
questions.a: Because the backtest and the live map are answering different questions. The backtest grades a 7-day-ahead forecast from historical complaints. The live map is an operational picture where an active fire or weapon detection on an area-tagged camera SHOULD push that locality up the board right now — that is a nowcast, not a forecast, and there is no way to backtest it because we have no historical anomaly stream. It is currently contributing 0 on screen anyway: active_anomalies is 0 for all 30 areas because no anomaly events exist and the 16 seeded videos have no area tag.

questions.q: Isn't this just fitting your own synthetic data generator?
questions.a: Partly yes, and that is the biggest caveat. 'Recency decay wins' is close to a test of how seed_synthetic.py generates data. What the backtest genuinely demonstrates is the METHODOLOGY — no-leakage rolling-origin folds, standard hotspot metrics, published baselines, a ceiling, and CIs — not real-world operational accuracy. The API returns that disclaimer as a field and the UI renders it verbatim at the bottom of the accuracy panel. We also have a self-check that proves the harness is real: flatten every weight and the model must collapse to a raw complaint count and exactly reproduce validation.py's independently-written frequency baseline. It does — 0.7420 == 0.7420.

questions.q: Eight folds is a small sample.
questions.a: Agreed, and it limits what we can claim. 'Not distinguishable' in our ablation is partly a statement about power, not about the component being useless. The fold count is capped at 26 in the API (?folds=N) if you want to trade window length for more folds. We also quote paired deltas rather than absolute levels, because levels drift as the 180-day synthetic window slides but the paired deltas are stable.

questions.q: How were the surges detected, and could you have planted them to be easy?
questions.a: They are planted — that is the point, it gives us ground truth — but the detection is fair. For each planted surge we score the model at the surge's END (so it has seen the surge build) and separately at the day BEFORE it began, and report the rank change. Maninagar 5→3, SG Highway 6→4, Satellite 10→9; all three in the top 10 during their surge week, 2/2 surges caught. We report per-SURGE, not per-area, because Satellite sits exactly on the top-10 boundary and lands on either side of it between runs as the 180-day window slides. Per-surge reproduces; per-area does not, and a headline that changes between runs is worse than useless.

questions.q: Show me the model. What are the actual coefficients?
questions.a: Click the ⓘ — the model card publishes all of them, and the API returns them in the same payload as the scores so nothing can drift. risk = prior + Σ w_severity · w_category · 0.5^(age/14 days) + 1.5 · active_anomalies, min-max scaled to 0-100. Severity: low 1, medium 2, high 3, critical 4. Category: murder ×2.0, body_offences ×1.6, assault ×1.5, chain_snatching ×1.3, burglary/narcotics ×1.2, vehicle_theft ×1.1, theft/cyber_fraud/prohibition ×1.0. Prior intensity: low 1, medium 3, high 6, from public NCRB/police/press reporting so a fresh deployment ranks sensibly before any live data arrives. Trend window 7 days. Bands: high ≥75, elevated ≥50, guarded ≥25, low below.

questions.q: Predictive policing has a well-known bias problem — you patrol where you predicted, generate more reports there, and the model confirms itself.
questions.a: Correct, and we do not claim to have solved it. Three things we do do: (1) the model is fed by CITIZEN complaints, not officer stops or arrests, which is the weaker of the two feedback loops but still a loop; (2) every score is decomposed on screen, so a supervisor can see a locality is ranked high because of a static prior rather than recent reports and discount it; (3) the static prior is published as a table with three coarse levels rather than hidden in learned weights. What we do NOT have is a drift monitor or a patrol-log feedback correction — patrol_logs are captured but are not fed back into the score. That is honest future work, not a shipped feature.

questions.q: How does the patrol router work? Is that a real optimiser or a straight line?
questions.a: Real, and pure stdlib so it works offline. Take the top-12 hotspots from the live model; assign them to units with a balanced greedy pass — walk hotspots by risk rank and give each to the unit whose running centroid is nearest, with a hard ceil(n/units) cap so one unit cannot hoard stops; then order each unit's stops with nearest-neighbour from the HQ depot and polish with 2-opt until no segment reversal shortens the tour. Distances are haversine. For a ~30-node city graph 2-opt is close enough to exact and needs no external routing API. Measured 0.05s for a 2-unit plan.

questions.q: Those routes are straight lines, not roads.
questions.a: Yes — deliberately. They are haversine great-circle legs between locality centroids, not turn-by-turn navigation. Adding OSRM or Google Directions would make the polylines follow roads and the km/ETA more accurate, but it would also make the whole feature require internet, which is the opposite of the deployment constraint. The ETA already bakes in a 25 km/h city patrol pace including observation stops, so the ~69 min for 28.8 km is an operational estimate, not a driving time.

questions.q: Does the patrol plan respect the category and time filters I set on the map?
questions.a: No, and that is a genuine limitation. patrol_routes() calls compute_risk() with no filters — it always plans over the all-time top-12 hotspots regardless of what the Reports layer is filtered to. If you filter to Chain snatching and then plan routes, you get the general crime routes, not chain-snatching routes.

questions.q: Why doesn't the 7/30/90-day selector change the risk forecast?
questions.a: Because the risk model has its own time weighting built in — a 14-day exponential half-life — so a hard window cut-off would double-count the recency handling and throw away the long tail the prior relies on. The UI reflects that: switching to the Risk forecast layer hides the category and window selectors entirely rather than leaving dead controls on screen.

questions.q: Your README says Hit-Rate@10 0.790 and PAI@10 2.37x but the screen says 0.78 and 2.35x.
questions.a: The synthetic window is 180 days ending at seed time, so as it slides the weekend uplift falls on different area/category/day combinations and the totals drift a little run to run (~1,970-2,001 complaints). The README documents that explicitly. Always read the number off the screen, never off the deck.

questions.q: Where does the Ahmedabad locality data come from?
questions.a: 30 named localities with real centroids in backend/app/constants/ahmedabad.py, and a per-area crime-intensity profile compiled from public NCRB / police / press reporting in seed_ahmedabad.py. The complaint stream itself is synthetic and disclosed as such on this very screen. The patrol depot is the real Cyber Crime Branch at Shahibaug (23.053, 72.593).

questions.q: What is that '10 linked cases' in the header, and why does Vatva's popup say Cases: 0?

Vatva has 263 complaints but no case has been opened against it yet — the 10 cases are concentrated elsewhere. headline.what: The architecture, not the screen: anomaly detection costs ZERO extra inference. Every keyframe already gets a CLIP vector for search; the watch scores that same existing vector against five per-class prompt ensembles, and separately scans the YOLO detections the pipeline already produced.
headline.why_impressive: It is genuinely clever engineering and it is the honest thing to talk about while the list is empty. No second model pass, no second GPU budget — anomaly detection is a nearly free by-product of building the search index. That is the answer to "can this scale to 5,000 city cameras?"

headline.what: The false-positive guard is a measured margin, not a raw threshold. A class only fires when it beats the best "normal scene" prompt by a calibrated margin — six negative prompts ("a normal city street with traffic", "calm traffic flowing on a road", …) anchor it.

A detector that screams on normal traffic is worse than no detector in a control room.

headline.what: The closed loop behind the card: a NEW event on a LIVE feed auto-spawns a geo-tagged case and dispatches the nearest patrol unit — the card then renders a "CASE #n AUTO-CREATED" chip that deep-links into the case workspace.
headline.why_impressive: Detection → case → dispatch with no human in the loop is the differentiator over a CCTV analytics box. The nearest-unit pick is real: it haversines each officer's most recent patrol check-in area against the incident area.

questions.q: Why is this screen empty? Is it broken?
questions.a: It is empty because nothing anomalous has happened. The DB has zero anomaly_events, and that is the correct output: all 16 loaded clips are ordinary Indian street, market and traffic CCTV — there is no fire, no weapon and no violence in any of them. 417 keyframes were scored and none crossed the margin. I would rather show you a detector that stays quiet on normal footage than one that fires on a red car.

questions.q: So you can't actually show me a detection?
questions.a: Not on this data — be straight about it. We can ingest a fire clip live (test_clips/fire/) and it will appear here, or you can look at the fire/smoke detection running inside the VisionScan search module. What this screen proves right now is the false-positive rate on 16 real feeds, which is zero.

questions.q: How does the detection work? Is it a separate model per class?
questions.a: No — it is hybrid and costs zero extra inference. Every keyframe already gets a CLIP vector for semantic search. The anomaly watch scores that SAME existing vector against five prompt ensembles (fire, smoke, accident, weapon, violence), each averaged over three phrasings so one odd wording cannot dominate. In parallel it scans the YOLO detections the pipeline already produced for weapon-class labels — COCO 'knife', plus a specialized fire/smoke weights file if present. Neither path adds a model pass.

questions.q: CLIP zero-shot on CCTV frames will fire on anything orange. How do you stop false positives?
questions.a: A measured margin, not a raw threshold. A class fires only when it beats the BEST of six negative 'normal scene' prompts — 'a normal city street with traffic', 'calm traffic flowing on a road', 'people walking peacefully on a sidewalk', and so on — by a calibrated margin (default 0.03, with per-class overrides, calibrated empirically via scripts/anomaly_selftest.py). The margin is what keeps ordinary street footage at effectively zero, and the empty screen in front of you is that calibration working on 417 real frames.

questions.q: Why do some alerts have a box drawn and others don't?
questions.a: Because only YOLO signals are localised. CLIP scores the WHOLE frame — it tells you the scene looks like a fire, not where in the frame the fire is — so a CLIP-sourced alert has null coordinates and the card deliberately draws no box rather than inventing one. YOLO signals carry a real bounding box, stored as 0..1 frame fractions so it renders correctly at any thumbnail size. I verified both paths: a YOLO stub with x1=0.25,y1=0.30,x2=0.62,y2=0.78 drew a box at exactly left 25% / top 30% / width 37% / height 48%, and a CLIP stub with null coordinates drew nothing.

questions.q: What stops a burning car generating a hundred alerts?
questions.a: Debouncing per (video_id, type). A new signal joins the most recent open event of the same type on the same feed if its last grouped frame is within 30 seconds; otherwise it opens a new event. The grouped event keeps the MAX confidence seen, bumps a peak_count, and the card renders that as 'N frames'. One incident, one card that grows — not a flood.

questions.q: What happens after an alert fires? Does someone have to notice it?
questions.a: No. A NEWLY created event on a LIVE feed above the notify threshold (0.70) pings the admins, and separately triggers the incident loop: it auto-creates a geo-tagged case and dispatches the nearest patrol unit — nearest computed by haversining each officer's most recent patrol check-in area against the incident area, with a fallback to any active officer so dispatch never silently no-ops. The card then shows a 'CASE #n AUTO-CREATED' chip that deep-links into the case workspace. Uploads of historical footage deliberately do NOT notify or auto-case, so reviewing old evidence does not spam the control room.

questions.q: What are the five classes and why those?
questions.a: fire, smoke, accident, weapon, violence. They are the five that (a) a city CCTV operator is actually watching for and (b) CLIP can separate from a normal street scene with a prompt ensemble. Note fire and smoke are separate classes on purpose — smoke usually precedes visible flame, so it is the earlier warning.

questions.q: How fast would an alert appear?
questions.a: It is written during ingestion, so within one keyframe interval of the frame being processed, and the UI polls every 5 seconds — I measured 4 poll requests in a 21-second window. The bottleneck is keyframe extraction rate, not the detector.

questions.q: Can an operator suppress a camera that keeps false-alarming?
questions.a: Not per-camera today, honestly. There are global and per-class confidence thresholds via environment variables (anomaly_conf_threshold, anomaly_class_thresholds, anomaly_weapon_yolo_conf) and an operator can dismiss individual alerts, which is audited — but there is no per-camera mute or zone mask in the UI. That is a real gap for a production control room.

broken: THE SCREEN IS EMPTY AND WILL BE EMPTY ON STAGE. Verified three ways: anomaly_events has 0 rows in the DB, all three status tabs return [] from the API, and /api/anomalies/summary returns {"new":0,"total":0}. Nothing is wrong with the code — the 16 loaded clips simply contain no anomalies. If you want a card on screen you must ingest test_clips/fire/fire_highrise_shanghai_01.ogv BEFORE the demo, which will change FEEDS 16→17 and INDEXED FRAMES 417→~440 on the dashboard. Decide which you care about more; do not discover this at 9am.

I COULD NOT VERIFY AN END-TO-END REAL DETECTION. Everything I report about the card layout, the box overlay geometry, the LIVE pill, the frame counter and the auto-created-case chip was verified by intercepting /api/anomalies in the browser and serving synthetic records in the exact shape the backend returns. The RENDERING path is proven correct; the DETECTION path is not proven on this data by me. Treat that distinction as load-bearing.

A SINGLE 429 REPLACES THE WHOLE LIST WITH AN ERROR. I hit "Could not load alerts. Retrying every 5s…" on the Acknowledged tab purely from rate limiting. Because this view polls every 5 seconds it is the heaviest per-minute consumer of the shared 120 req/min bucket after the health/videos pollers, so it is the most likely screen to trip it. It does self-heal on the next poll.
No per-camera mute, no zone masking, no threshold control in the UI. Everything is environment-variable configuration. Do not offer to "tune it live".

There is no way to see historical/resolved alerts beyond the three status tabs — no date filter, no search, no pagination (the API caps at 50 by default, 200 max, and the UI never passes a limit). Fine at zero events; would matter at a thousand.
The Dismissed tab's empty state renders as "No Dismissed alerts." with the tab name interpolated — grammatically odd on a projector. Leave the New tab selected.

One stubbed thumbnail (frame from video 56) failed to load in my run while others succeeded, most likely a 429 on the static path. If a card ever shows a blank frame on stage, it is a transient fetch, not a missing thumbnail.

questions.q: Is the citizen view just the same page with buttons hidden?

questions.q: Can an officer close a case?
questions.a: No, and it is enforced twice: the Close button is not rendered for role=officer, and POST /api/cases/31/close with an officer token returns 403. Only lead and admin can close (require_role("lead")).

questions.q: Where does the citizen satisfaction rating show up?
questions.a: Honest answer: only as an aggregate. Ratings are stored per case (5 ratings: 4,4,5,3,5) and surface as the Dashboard KPI "Avg rating 4.2/5 (5)". The case workspace never shows the rating a case received — for staff there is no rating element at all, and for the citizen the star widget is an input that always starts empty. Do not promise "open a closed case and see its rating" on stage; it is not there.

questions.q: How do you assign a case to an officer?
questions.a: Today, via the API only: POST /api/cases/{id}/assign {"user_ids":[19]} (lead+ only, 25ms, writes an assign_case audit row and notifies the assignee). There is no button for it in the UI. Cases inherit the creator's team at creation, which is how the officer sees them at all.

questions.q: Is the timeline a real audit log or a rendering of the case fields?
questions.a: Real table. audit_log rows are written by the API on create_case, close_case, add_evidence, citizen_visibility, assign_case, rate_case, triage_complaint, exports and admin actions, each with actor_id and timestamp; the case Timeline tab is a filtered view of it and the Admin → security tab shows the same log unfiltered.

questions.q: Why do the seeded cases only have two timeline entries?
questions.a: Because the seed writes only the two audit events that actually happened (created, closed). Everything you do live appends properly — my test case ended with 4 entries after add_evidence, citizen_visibility and close. If you want a fat timeline on stage, add evidence and flip visibility before opening the tab.

questions.q: A case converted from a complaint has no 'case created' entry in its timeline — why?
questions.a: Correct, and it is a gap. The triage endpoint audits triage_complaint against the complaint entity, not create_case against the new case, so a converted case's audit trail starts at its first post-creation action. The Complaints screen still links the two ("View case #38").

questions.q: What happens if two officers edit the same case at once?
questions.a: Nothing stops them — there is no optimistic locking or field-level versioning. Evidence and messages are append-only so they merge fine; close/visibility are last-write-wins and both writes land in the audit log.

questions.q: Does rendering 2001 rows not kill the browser?
questions.a: Measured, not guessed: 2.79s to first paint, all 2001 rows in the DOM, 2.54s to scroll to the bottom, no crash, 1.06 MB payload in ~50ms. It works — it just will not scale to a real station's 200k complaints without pagination.

questions.q: Can a citizen see other citizens' complaints?
questions.a: The query is WHERE citizen_id = ?, so no. But be careful how you phrase it on stage: in this demo database all 2001 synthetic complaints are owned by the one demo citizen account, so the citizen login shows 2001 rows. That is seed design, not a leak.

questions.q: What actually happens when you tick 'Open a case from this complaint'?
questions.a: One transaction: the complaint is updated (severity, priority, response, status='assigned'), a case row is inserted carrying the complaint's title, description, complainant id and the chosen severity/priority, then the complaint is flipped to status='converted' with case_id set. The citizen gets a notification with the response message; the assigned team gets one too.

questions.q: Is the complaint→case link bidirectional?
questions.a: Yes. The complaint row gains "View case #N", and the case row stores complaint_id. The only gap is the audit trail: conversion is logged as triage_complaint against the complaint, so the new case's own timeline has no create_case entry.

questions.q: Who can triage?

questions.q: Where did 2001 complaints come from — is this real data?
questions.a: Synthetic, deterministic, and honestly labelled: the seed derives area-wise distributions from public NCRB/press reporting (docs/AHMEDABAD_CRIME_DATA.md) and spreads them over the last ~6 months (2026-02-20 to 2026-08-19). Category mix: assault 492, theft 318, vehicle_theft 301, cyber_fraud 273, body_offences 251, chain_snatching 214, murder 61, burglary 47, narcotics 41.

questions.q: Which of these six tabs are worth opening in front of judges?
questions.a: monitoring (live CPU/RAM/DB/requests/errors + model load state), data (four exports that really download and are audited), broadcast (visible platform-wide effect), teams (grounds the RBAC story). users is a thin 5-row list with a form that crashes on invalid input. security is worth describing but its two buttons are both destructive.

questions.q: Is the lockdown switch real?
questions.a: Yes — LockdownMiddleware is in the request path. When the flag is on, everything except /api/health, /api/auth/login, /api/admin/* and requests carrying a valid admin JWT is rejected with HTTP 423 "CityShield is in emergency lockdown". I deliberately did NOT enable it during testing because other people were on the same stack; the state is persisted in app_settings with a 2s cache, and lifting it is one click.

questions.q: What does 'Sign out all my sessions' actually do?
questions.a: Increments the user's token_version, which invalidates every JWT ever issued to that account — including the one in the presenter's browser. You will be dropped to the login screen mid-demo. Same mechanism fires automatically when an admin changes someone's role or deactivates them, which is the correct behaviour but makes this button a bad thing to click on stage.

questions.q: Every login row shows the same IP, 172.20.0.3 — is that real?
questions.a: That is the nginx container's address. nginx forwards X-Real-IP but the backend logs request.client.host, so browser logins all collapse to one internal IP. The same shortcut means the 120 req/min rate limiter buckets every browser user together — which is why testing agents kept hitting 429. Both fix in one place: trust X-Forwarded-For behind the proxy.

questions.q: Is the audit log complete enough to hand to an auditor?
questions.a: It covers case lifecycle (create/close/evidence/visibility/assign/rate), complaint triage, user creation and updates, and every data export, each with actor id and timestamp — 57 rows currently, and exports show up in it within seconds. Gaps: reads are not audited, a complaint→case conversion is logged against the complaint rather than the new case, and there is no tamper-evidence (it is an ordinary SQLite table an admin could edit).

questions.q: Can a non-admin reach the admin API by guessing URLs?
questions.a: No. GET /api/users, GET /api/admin/system, GET /api/admin/security-events, GET /api/admin/export/*, POST /api/users, POST /api/teams and POST /api/notifications/broadcast all return 403 "Insufficient permissions" for lead, officer and citizen tokens — I ran all of them. GET /api/teams is deliberately open to any signed-in user (the team picker needs it).

questions.q: Only one team and five users — is the RBAC just hard-coded?
questions.a: No, it is data-driven: roles are a column on users, team membership is a foreign key, and case access is computed from assigned_team_id plus the case_assignments table. It is a small dataset, not a small mechanism — adding a second team through Admin → teams and moving the officer would immediately change what he can see.

broken: Admin → users → "Add staff user": submitting with ANY invalid field (blank form, malformed email, password under 6 characters) crashes the entire React app to the "Something went wrong" error boundary and needs a page reload. Root cause is one line — the 422 body's `detail` is an array of pydantic error objects and CreateUserModal renders it directly as a React child (frontend/src/components/platform/AdminView.jsx, the setErr(e?.response?.data?.detail ...) call in CreateUserModal). A one-line coercion to a string fixes it, but it needs a frontend image rebuild, which I did not do because other agents are on this stack. Until then: do not open that form on stage.
Admin → security → "Sign out all my sessions" will log the presenter out instantly. Do not click.
Admin → security → "Activate lockdown" blocks every non-admin request platform-wide with HTTP 423. Safe to describe, risky to click; if clicked, "Lift lockdown" restores service immediately.

Admin → users is thin: 5 accounts including "QA Probe", a citizen created by another testing agent. There is no delete or deactivate control, and no role-change control in the UI (the API supports PATCH role).
Admin → teams has exactly 1 team with 2 members. Expanding it is fine; do not click the X next to Const. A. Patel — removing him from the team empties his case list and breaks the RBAC demo.

Recent broadcasts was empty before my test and now contains one deactivated row titled "QA test advisory — ignore". Delete-broadcast does not exist, so that row will be visible in the history panel during the demo.
Login-attempt IPs are all 172.20.0.3 (the nginx container), not real client addresses.

Shared 120 req/min rate limit: with a couple of browser tabs plus the 5s monitoring poller, the API starts returning 429 and screens silently render empty (the officer's case list showed 0 cases during one rate-limited run when the API had 10). Close spare tabs before the demo.

headline.what: Open the SAME case in two browsers — admin and citizen — side by side. Admin sees 5 tabs and 5 evidence rows; the citizen sees 2 tabs and 1 evidence row, because the API returns one row for that token.
headline.why_impressive: This is the demo that answers "is it really role-based?" without opening a terminal: the difference is in the payload, not the stylesheet.

questions.q: Is this actually role-based access control, or just hidden buttons?
questions.a: Both layers exist, and the server layer is the real one. Measured with real tokens: officer POST /api/users → 403, POST /api/cases → 403, POST /api/cases/31/close → 403, POST /api/complaints/{id}/triage → 403, GET /api/admin/system → 403, GET /api/admin/export/cases.csv → 403. Citizen additionally: GET /api/cases/31/timeline → 403 "Staff only", GET /api/analytics/summary → 403, POST evidence → 403, and a case they do not own → 403 "No access to this case". The UI hiding is convenience; removing it would change nothing about what the API permits.

questions.q: Give me one concrete forbidden call and its status code.
questions.a: POST /api/users with the officer's JWT returns HTTP 403 with body {"detail":"Insufficient permissions"}. The same call with the admin's JWT returns 200. It is enforced by a FastAPI dependency, require_role("admin"), on the route itself — not by the router and not by the frontend.

questions.q: How are the four roles ranked?
questions.a: citizen < officer < lead < admin, compared by role_rank(). Endpoints declare a minimum: evidence and citizen-visibility need officer; case creation, closing and complaint triage need lead; user/team management, exports, system status, security events and broadcasts need admin. Reads on a case additionally pass through can_access_case(), which checks team membership, personal assignment, or complainant ownership plus the citizen-visible flag.

questions.q: Can an officer from another station read this station's cases?
questions.a: No — the case query filters on assigned_team_id or an explicit row in case_assignments. There is only one team in this demo database, so you have to take the query on trust or create a second team live in Admin → teams to show it.

questions.q: What stops a citizen from spamming an investigating officer?
questions.a: A server-side cap of one message per case: the second POST returns 403 "Citizens may send only one message per case". The UI even changes the placeholder to "One message allowed…".

questions.q: If you demote someone, do their existing sessions keep working?
questions.a: No. PATCH /api/users/{id} bumps that user's token_version whenever role or active changes, and every JWT carries the version it was minted with, so all outstanding tokens for that user stop validating immediately. The same mechanism backs the "Sign out all my sessions" button.

questions.q: Where is authorisation implemented — could a new endpoint forget it?
questions.a: Yes, it could, and that is the honest weakness: it is per-route dependencies (require_role / get_current_user + get_case_or_403), not a global default-deny policy. A newly added route with no dependency would be open to any signed-in user.

questions.q: Are the demo passwords the real security model?
questions.a: No — admin123 / officer123 exist because judges need to log in in five seconds. Passwords are bcrypt-hashed, sessions are HS256 JWTs with an expiry and a token_version, failed logins are rate-limited to 10/min per IP and recorded with IP and outcome in the security tab. The weak passwords are demo seed data, gated by a setting.

broken: The citizen account owns all 2001 complaints in this database, so "My complaints" shows 2001 rows. That is seed design, not an access-control failure — but do not open that screen while saying "a citizen only sees their own complaints", because it looks exactly like a leak.

GET /api/teams is readable by every signed-in role including citizens (it returns team name, station and member count). Deliberate — the team dropdowns need it — but it is the one endpoint that does not follow the pattern.
Authorisation is per-route, so a future endpoint added without a require_role dependency would be open to any authenticated user. There is no global default-deny.

Officer and lead have identical navigation, so the officer-vs-lead difference only becomes visible inside a case (no Close button) or on Complaints (no Triage button). Point at those two specifically or the distinction is invisible.

Case #38 is assigned to the officer (Const. A. Patel) but not to the lead's team, so the officer sees 10 cases while the lead sees 9. That asymmetry is my test artefact, not a bug — but if a judge counts cards across two logins, that is why the numbers differ.

During testing, the admin account's UI language was flipped to Hindi by another agent (it is a stored per-user preference, so it follows the account across browsers). If the interface comes up in Devanagari, switch it back with the language selector in the header before the demo starts.

name: Arbiter — Legal Intelligence (Section Lookup · FIR Draft · Legal Q&A)
route: Sign in at http://localhost:8080 as admin@city.gov / admin123 → top nav, 5th tab "Arbiter". The three tabs are mode buttons inside the panel: Section Lookup (default) / FIR Draft / Legal Q&A. Officer role also sees this tab.
one_liner: An offline RAG legal assistant over a 25-section IPC / IT Act 2000 / CrPC corpus that ranks applicable sections, drafts a registration-format FIR, and answers plain-language legal questions — no internet and no API key involved.

headline.what: Type a plain-language incident and get ranked statutes with punishments back in ~70 ms, fully offline. "Caller impersonating a bank official obtained the OTP and transferred Rs 2,40,000" returns IT Act 66C Identity theft at 52%, 66D Cheating by personation at 37%, 72 Breach of confidentiality at 35% — exactly the three sections an Ahmedabad cyber cell would file.
headline.why_impressive: It is semantic retrieval, not keyword grep: the words "identity theft", "personation" and "confidentiality" never appear in the query. And the amber badge in the corner says "Offline mode" — this runs on a laptop in a police station with the network unplugged.
headline.exact_steps: Arbiter tab → Section Lookup (already selected) → paste the query into the textarea → click "Find Sections". Result renders in under a second.

headline.what: FIR Draft: one narrative paragraph plus four fields produces a complete registration-format FIR with numbered BRIEF FACTS / APPLICABLE LEGAL PROVISIONS / PRAYER sections, complainant and accused filled in, signature and P.S. lines, plus a provenance badge reading "Template draft" and an amber disclaimer.
headline.why_impressive: It is a document an officer could hand across the counter, generated in 71 ms, and it is explicitly labelled as machine-drafted rather than pretending to be a filed FIR. The section chips above the draft are the same retrieval that powers Section Lookup, so the citations are grounded in a real corpus and cannot be hallucinated.
headline.exact_steps: Click "FIR Draft" → paste the incident into the textarea → fill the four inputs (Complainant / Accused / Place / Date-time) → click "Draft FIR".

headline.what: Mode switching preserves the textarea, so the same facts flow through all three tabs without retyping: describe the incident in Section Lookup, click FIR Draft, click Draft FIR.
headline.why_impressive: It is the actual officer workflow in three clicks, and it lets you show all three capabilities on one set of facts inside 30 seconds of stage time.

headline.what: Legal Q&A answers a citizen's question with a cited, plain-language answer plus the full section cards underneath and citation chips.
headline.why_impressive: Same corpus, different audience — the panel doubles as a public-facing legal helpdesk, which is the "citizen portal" half of CityShield's story.
headline.exact_steps: Click "Legal Q&A" → type the question → click "Get Answer".

headline.what: The "Offline mode · 25 sections" badge itself, explained.
headline.why_impressive: Judges expect an LLM wrapper. This is ChromaDB with the built-in MiniLM ONNX embedder, persisted locally, so retrieval is real vector search with zero external calls; Gemini is an optional polish layer that is currently off (llm_online=false) and the system degrades to a deterministic, citation-grounded template rather than breaking.

questions.q: That badge says "Offline mode". So there is no AI here — it is a lookup table?
questions.a: No. Retrieval is real semantic search: the 25 sections are embedded once into a persistent ChromaDB collection with Chroma's built-in MiniLM ONNX embedder and queried by cosine similarity. The proof is that "Caller impersonating a bank official obtained the OTP" returns IT Act 66C "Identity theft" at 52% when the words identity and theft never appear in the query. What is offline is the *generation* step — with no Gemini key set (llm_online=false) the prose is composed from a deterministic template around the retrieved sections, rather than written by an LLM.

questions.q: What changes if you plug in a Gemini key?
questions.a: Three things, all visible in the UI. The badge flips to green "Gemini online"; the FIR provenance chip flips from "Template draft" to "Gemini draft"; and the language dropdown starts working, because translation is delegated to the same LLM bridge. Retrieval does not change at all — Gemini is only allowed to compose prose around sections that retrieval already found, and there is an output validator that rejects the generation and falls back to the template if the model cites a section that was not in the retrieved set. That is a deliberate anti-hallucination guard, not an accident of being offline.

questions.q: How do I know it will not invent a section number?
questions.a: Structurally it cannot. `suggest_sections` returns rows straight out of the vector store — every citation is a row in the corpus JSON. For the LLM path, `guards.validate_output` checks the generated text against the set of citations that were actually retrieved and discards the generation if it cites anything else. The corpus is 25 hand-written entries in backend/app/arbiter/corpus/legal_corpus.json, so the failure mode is silence, not fiction.

questions.q: Only 25 sections? The IPC alone has 511.
questions.a: Correct, and that is the honest ceiling. The 25 are a curated cyber-crime-first set — 10 IT Act 2000 sections, 12 IPC, 3 CrPC — chosen for the Ahmedabad Cyber Crime Branch's actual caseload. It has real gaps: no 498A, no 304B dowry death, no 363/364A kidnapping, no 376, no NI Act 138, and no BNS 2023 at all. Ask it about kidnapping for ransom and it confidently returns IPC 392 Robbery. Widening it is a data task not an engineering task — the ingestion is `coll.upsert` over a JSON file and re-indexing is idempotent on restart. Notably CrimeGPT's Suggest Sections tab already carries a separate BNS 2023 / BNSS catalogue, so the two together cover both statutory eras.

questions.q: Why does chain snatching return "IT Act 66C Identity theft" and "IPC 354D Stalking"?
questions.a: Because retrieval returns exactly top-k with no relevance floor — it always hands back 6 rows even when only two are above 30% similarity. The match percentage on each card is the honest signal and the bad hits sit at 17-21%. The right product fix is a score cutoff (drop anything under ~0.30) which would have shown two sections instead of six here. It is one line in `store.retrieve`; it is not in yet.

questions.q: Does it tell me whether the offence is cognizable and bailable? That is the first thing a duty officer needs.
questions.a: The data is there and the API returns it — POST /api/legal/sections gives cognizable and bailable per section — but the UI card does not render either field today. It shows citation, match %, title, summary and punishment only. That is a genuine gap between the backend and the front end, not something we are hiding.

questions.q: You offer Hindi and Gujarati in the dropdown. Show me a Hindi answer.
questions.a: It will come back in English, and I would rather say that than click it. Translation runs through the same LLM bridge as generation, and with no key configured the bridge returns None and the template falls through in English. The interface chrome is fully translated in all three languages — 706 keys — but the generated legal text is not. Do not demo that dropdown.

questions.q: Is this legally safe? What if an officer files it as-is?
questions.a: Two layers. Every FIR carries a "Template draft" or "Gemini draft" provenance chip so nobody can mistake which produced it, plus an amber disclaimer and an in-document NOTE requiring the IO to verify facts and section applicability before registration. And Arbiter never writes to a case — it produces a draft in the browser. The section suggestion is advisory; registration remains a human act.

questions.q: How fast is it, and what does it cost to run?
questions.a: Measured server-side over 5 runs each: section lookup 69 ms median, FIR draft 71 ms, Q&A 60 ms. Cost is zero — no API calls, no GPU. The whole legal brain is a ChromaDB directory on disk.

questions.q: Prompt injection — the incident text is user-supplied. What stops "ignore your instructions"?
questions.a: Every user string goes through `guards.sanitize_user_text` and is then wrapped in explicit <<<UNTRUSTED_…>>> fences before it reaches the model, and the system prompt states that fenced content is data and never an instruction. On top of that the output validator rejects any generation citing sections outside the retrieved set. Offline today none of it is exercised because there is no model — but the guard is in the code path, not bolted on later.

broken: cognizable and bailable never render in the UI. The API returns them per section; ArbiterPanel's SectionCard draws only citation / match% / title / summary / punishment. Do not promise a judge the bailability flag on this screen.
The language dropdown on FIR Draft and Legal Q&A is dead offline. Selecting हिन्दी or ગુજરાતી returns byte-identical English (measured). Presenter should not click it.
No relevance floor — retrieval always returns exactly top_k. "Two men snatched a gold chain" returns IT Act 66C Identity theft and IPC 354D Stalking at 17-21% alongside the correct IPC 379/392.

DO NOT DEMO: kidnapping / ransom. "Ransom demand after kidnapping a minor boy from school" returns IPC 392 Robbery, IPC 379 Theft, CrPC 41. There is no kidnapping or abduction section in the 25-item corpus.

DO NOT DEMO: dowry / matrimonial cruelty. "Man assaulted his wife demanding dowry" returns IPC 323, 506, 307 and then IT Act 67B (child sexually explicit material) at 22%. There is no 498A or 304B in the corpus and the 67B hit looks terrible on a projector.

DO NOT DEMO: "Someone is sending me threatening messages on WhatsApp every day" in Legal Q&A — it cites IT Act 66F Cyber terrorism (punishment up to life imprisonment) as the second-most-relevant provision.

Legal Q&A does not actually answer the question asked; it lists the three most relevant sections with their punishments and a closing line. Asking "is this bailable?" gets you sections but never a yes or no. Frame it as "cited legal grounding", not "a chatbot".

The FIR draft is stamped with the server clock, which runs UTC inside the container. At 00:52 IST on 20 Aug the draft read "Date of report : 2026-08-19 19:22". Harmless for a morning demo (10:00 IST = 04:30 UTC, same date) but the date will look a day behind if anyone demos late at night.
Nothing crashed. Zero pageerrors and zero /api/ responses ≥400 across every Arbiter interaction tested.

name: CrimeGPT — case-document generator
route: Sign in as admin@city.gov / admin123 → top nav, 6th tab "CrimeGPT". Case picker is top-right (4 open cases). Four tabs: Data Pool / Suggest Sections / Documents / Case Diary. Data Pool has three sub-tabs: Parties / Seizures / Statements. Use case "#29 · Digital-arrest cyber-fraud ring busted" — it is the only one with a populated pool.
one_liner: Enter the case facts once into a unified data pool, then generate all seven statutory Indian-police documents as branded, versioned PDFs — each one drawing the slice of the pool it actually needs.

headline.what: Seven statutory documents from one data pool, in seven clicks. I generated every one of Purvani Chargesheet, Medical Treatment Letter, Remand Request (BNSS s.187), Seizure Receipt, Court Custody Letter, Accused Panchanama and Face Identification Form — all seven downloaded, all seven opened cleanly, 51 ms median server-side.
headline.why_impressive: This is the paperwork that eats an investigating officer's week. The officer types the accused, the victim, the muddamal and the statements exactly once and the whole statutory file falls out, correctly formatted, on Cyber Crime Branch letterhead, with FIR number and police station in the header of every page.
headline.exact_steps: CrimeGPT tab → case #29 → "Documents" tab → click "Generate PDF" on each card. Each fires a browser download named e.g. accused_panchanama_case29_v1_en.pdf.

headline.what: The documents are genuinely different, not one template with a swapped title. The Panchanama pulls the seizures in as "Articles Found on the Accused" and prints a physical-description line per accused; the Medical Letter names only the single person to be examined and asks for an MLC plus FSL sample preservation; the Face Identification Form emits a photograph box per accused with Complexion/Build/Height/Face-shape blanks and a "VisionScan facial-match reference" field; the Seizure Receipt is a 5-column panchnama with date, place and both panch witnesses per item.
headline.why_impressive: That last one is the platform tie-in a judge will notice: the face-ID form has a slot for the similarity score and camera timestamp coming out of VisionScan, so the AI evidence lands in the statutory record rather than in a screenshot.

headline.what: Every generation is auto-written to the Case Diary (Roznamcha) with version, officer name and timestamp — case #29 carries 18 entries covering parties added, seizures recorded, statements taken and each document version generated.
headline.why_impressive: It is an audit trail nobody has to remember to write. Adding an accused writes "Accused 'Rakesh Bhanushali' added to the case file"; generating a PDF writes "Purvani Chargesheet v2 generated by Station Admin". Chain of custody by construction.

headline.what: Suggest Sections works off BNS 2023 with the pre-2023 IPC cross-reference printed next to it, plus BNSS procedure and the exact terms that matched.
headline.why_impressive: India switched criminal codes on 1 July 2024 and most officers still think in IPC. Showing "BNS 318 — Cheating (IPC 415/420)" side by side is the bridge, and printing the matched terms means the officer can see why it fired instead of trusting a black box.
headline.exact_steps: "Suggest Sections" tab → paste the narrative in the box → click Suggest. Use the exact narrative in the inputs section — the built-in case description only scores 2.

headline.what: The two fixes shipped today, both verified in a generated PDF: the language line now reads "Language: EN (requested HI — translation needs an LLM key)" instead of falsely claiming HI, and the Station Seal now has a real 4.6 cm × 2.6 cm bordered box underneath the label.
headline.why_impressive: The first is an integrity fix on an evidentiary record — the document states what it actually is. The second is the kind of physical-world detail that tells a police audience someone thought about the rubber stamp.

questions.q: Can it produce a Hindi or Gujarati document? The interface is trilingual.
questions.a: The interface is, the PDF body is not, and I want to be exact about why. Two separate things are missing. First, translation: the narrative goes through the Arbiter LLM bridge, which is offline with no Gemini key, so the English text passes through unchanged — and as of today the PDF states this on its face rather than lying, it prints "Language: EN (requested HI — translation needs an LLM key)". Second, and this one no API key fixes: ReportLab does no Indic text shaping. We bundle Noto Sans Devanagari and Gujarati and they embed correctly — you can put a Hindi name in the pool and it appears in the PDF — but ReportLab lays glyphs out in logical order, and Devanagari requires reordering. The short-i vowel sign ि is stored after its consonant and must be drawn before it. So चेन स्नैचिंग comes out as चेन स्नैचगि, डिजिटल as डजिटिल, त्वरित as त्वरति. Base letters and most matras are fine; anything with ि is visibly wrong. The correct fix is a shaping engine — HarfBuzz via uharfbuzz, or rendering through WeasyPrint/Pango instead of ReportLab — which is a real piece of work, not a config flag. So today: use English for the document body. The UI, the case data and the officer's workflow are trilingual; the printed evidentiary record is English.

questions.q: So a judge should not ask you to print a Hindi chargesheet.
questions.a: They can, and I would show it — it will print an English body with an accurate label saying that is what happened. What I will not do is put Hindi paragraphs in an evidentiary document and let broken conjuncts go into a court file. Stamping "Language: HI" on an English document was a false statement on a record and we fixed that this morning; printing garbled Devanagari would be the same mistake wearing a different hat.

questions.q: These look like Word templates with mail-merge. What is the AI part?
questions.a: The document assembly is deterministic by design — you do not want a language model inventing the wording of a remand application. Two AI pieces sit around it. The section suggester scores the narrative against a curated BNS 2023 / BNSS / BSA catalogue and prints the terms that matched, so the officer sees the reasoning. And the pool itself is fed by the rest of the platform — the Face Identification Form has a slot for VisionScan's facial-match reference, similarity score and camera timestamp. The value here is not generative prose, it is that seven statutory documents share one source of truth and stay consistent with each other.

questions.q: How do you know the BNS section numbers are right? Wrong sections in front of police judges are fatal.
questions.a: They were cross-checked against the enacted BNS 2023, BNSS 2023 and BSA 2023 texts, and the source file says so at the top with a standing warning. Where a mapping is broad the entry carries verify=True and the UI surfaces a "verify before use" caution. Landmark judgments are attached only where squarely on point — otherwise the list is left empty rather than risk a bad cite. And the IPC cross-references are labelled as the closest pre-2023 equivalent for officer familiarity, not a claim of identical scope. Every card also carries "Always verify the exact clause against the bare act before filing."

questions.q: Why did my narrative return zero sections?
questions.a: Because the suggester is a deterministic substring matcher over 30 offence patterns, not a semantic model — deliberately, so it is auditable and can show you exactly which words fired. The cost is that it misses paraphrase. I measured it: "posing as a CBI officer… digital arrest… mule accounts" scores zero, because none of cheating/fraud/otp/phishing/personation/fake/scam appear. Add "online fraud" and "OTP" to the same facts and it scores 10 across three patterns. That is a real gap, and the fix is the same ChromaDB retrieval Arbiter already uses — the infrastructure is already in the repo, it just is not wired to this catalogue yet.

questions.q: Where do the generated PDFs live? Can they be tampered with?
questions.a: Each generation is recorded server-side with case, doc type, language, an incrementing version, the generating officer's id and a timestamp, and it writes an immutable Case Diary entry. Versions never overwrite — the chargesheet on case 29 is at v9 because I regenerated it during load testing, and all nine are in the history. What is not there yet is a content hash or signature on the stored bytes, so this is tamper-evident at the metadata level, not cryptographically tamper-proof.

questions.q: How fast, and can it do a whole station's caseload?
questions.a: 51 ms median server-side for the 2-page chargesheet, measured over 5 runs; the single-page documents are faster. The whole file of seven documents for one case is well under a second of compute. Generation is pure CPU with no external calls, so throughput is bounded by the box, not by an API quota.

questions.q: What happens if generation fails?
questions.a: Right now, nothing visible — the grid catches the error and drops it, so the button stops spinning and no file arrives. That is the weakest thing on this screen and it is a two-line fix. The backend does the right thing (returns a 500 with the reason); the front end just does not show it.

broken: Version History rows and Case Diary entries STILL claim "HI" / "GU" for documents whose body is English. The fix landed in the PDF header only. Source: backend/app/crimegpt/routes.py:199 writes f"({language.upper()})" into the diary narrative, and svc.record_document stores the requested language, which the history row renders. Font embeds fine (AAAAAA+NotoSansDevanagari-Regular in the PDF font table); ReportLab does no shaping so the short-i vowel sign is drawn on the wrong side of its consonant. Do not type Devanagari or Gujarati into the pool, and do not print an Indic document on stage.

questions.q: Is this a real corpus or did you type 33 fake documents?
questions.a: Real, and every one is clickable. I verified all 33 source links: 32 return HTTP 200 to a script, and the 33rd plus nine others I opened in an actual browser — all 200 with the right page title. The Acts point at indiacode.nic.in PDFs, the judgments at indiankanoon, the CERT-In directions at cert-in.org.in, the Gujarat Police Innovation Challenge at gujaratinformation.gujarat.gov.in. Seven of those links were broken and were fixed today. Click any Source button you like.

questions.q: The badge says 53 documents but you said the corpus is 33.
questions.a: Both are true and the difference is the point. 33 is the bundled offline corpus that ships with the image and works with the network unplugged. The other 20 came in live from PIB Gujarat's RSS the last time someone clicked Refresh feeds. The header badge and the DOCUMENTS INDEXED tile show the union; the tile also breaks it out as "20 live". Unplug the network and you still have 33 searchable documents.

questions.q: SOURCE HEALTH says 1 of 4 feeds live. What is wrong with the other three?
questions.a: I checked each from inside the container. The two RBI feeds return HTTP 418 — RBI's bot protection rejects any non-browser client, so those two are structurally dead for a server-side fetcher and would need a headless browser or a paid data source. The PIB all-India feed returns HTTP 200 with a valid but EMPTY RSS channel — that is upstream, PIB simply publishes nothing on Regid=0. PIB Gujarat returns 20 items reliably, which happens to be the regionally relevant one. The panel shows 1/4 rather than hiding it, which is the honest thing for a feed-health tile to do.

questions.q: What is the difference between the "linked", "same family" and "similar" badges on related documents?
questions.a: Three different mechanisms, deliberately labelled so you know which one fired. "linked" at 100% is a curated hand-authored relationship in the corpus — the I4C e-Zero FIR notification is explicitly linked to its Gujarat implementation and to the 1930 helpline. "same family" means the documents share a statutory lineage — IT Act 2000 to the e-Zero FIR notification. "similar" with a percentage is pure vector similarity from the embedding store. So a judge can tell curated ground truth from machine inference at a glance, rather than us presenting both as "related".

questions.q: Search returns 24 results for everything. Type gibberish and it still returns 24.
questions.a: Correct, and that is the sharpest flaw on this screen. Retrieval returns exactly k results with no relevance floor — "zzzzqqq nothing" comes back with 24 documents at 15-16%. The score badge on each card is the honest signal and it collapses to noise, but the count line does not. The fix is a similarity cutoff in the search service, roughly a five-line change, and it is not in yet. What the ranking does get right is order: real queries put the right document first at 55-62% every time.

questions.q: Why does "Central" say 24 documents when the tile says Central 27?
questions.a: The search request is capped at k=24 for page performance, so 27 central documents get truncated to the first 24 and the count line reports what was returned rather than what matched. Same for Gujarat's 26. There is no pagination on this panel — you narrow with a query or a filter instead. The insights tile is the source of truth for corpus totals.

questions.q: You clicked Refresh and the "last fetch" timestamp did not move.
questions.a: Because that tile is MAX(fetched_at) across documents — it is the time the newest document entered the index, not the time we last polled. The refresh genuinely ran (it reported "Fetched 20, 0 new") and found nothing new, so no document got a new fetched_at. Mislabelled tile, not a broken refresh. The per-feed last_attempt timestamps in the API did update.

questions.q: Is the AI summary generated by a model?
questions.a: Not by an LLM — llm_online is false. It is extractive: it selects and condenses sentences from the stored document body and renders them as bullets, in 15 ms, offline. If a Gemini key were configured the badge would flip to "Gemini summaries" and the same button would produce an abstractive summary in the selected language. Today the language selector changes only the button label; the text stays English. I would rather tell you that than click it and hope.

questions.q: Who can refresh the feeds? Could a citizen trigger 20 outbound requests?
