questions.q: VisionScan has Text search and Object search — what is the difference?
questions.a: Text embeds the WHOLE FRAME with CLIP and finds scenes: one 512-d vector per keyframe, cosine-matched against the embedded sentence. It answers "where does this situation happen". Object runs a YOLO label filter over the detections table first, and when the phrase isn't one of YOLO's classes it falls back to per-detection CLIP on the cropped object regions — that's what lets "red car" find a specific car and draw a box on it. Concretely on this data: plain text "red car" returns 1 fuzzy scene; per-object returns 24 individually-boxed cars.

questions.q: What does "Grouping moments" actually do?
questions.a: Two different things depending on the search, and that is deliberate. For text, YOLO-label and face search it clusters frames from the same camera that are within event_gap_sec (6 s) of each other and keeps the highest-scoring one as the representative — so 40 raw frames of one person loitering become 8 distinct moments. For per-object (region) search it groups on track_id instead, because two different red cars visible in the same second are two results, not one; time-clustering would wrongly merge them.

questions.q: Those scores are only 25–33%. Is that a bad match?
questions.a: Those are raw CLIP cosine similarities, and for text-to-image CLIP the usable range is compressed — roughly 0.18 is noise and 0.33 is a strong hit on this data. What matters is the ranking and the relative floor: we cut anything below 0.22 absolute and below 0.88× the top hit. That is why "underwater coral reef scuba diver" returns zero instead of a page of 0.20s. We do not present the raw number as a confidence probability.

questions.q: Can it handle negation — "a street with NO people"?
questions.a: No, and this is a real limitation of CLIP, not a bug in our code. CLIP has no logical operators; it embeds the bag of concepts, so "no people" pulls toward frames about people and streets. Measured: "empty street with no people" returns 5 hits and all 5 contain detected people. Worse, per-object "no people" returns 60 hits topped by stop signs and a fire hydrant. The honest workaround is structural, not semantic: use Object search for "person" with grouping on and read the frames where the count is zero — the detections table can answer absence, the embedding cannot.

questions.q: How large is the index, and would this scale to a real city?
questions.a: Right now: 417 keyframes, 3,362 detections, 956 faces, 1,409 tracks across 16 cameras, in FAISS with SQLite for metadata. Warm text search is 80 ms median. FAISS flat search is linear, so at city scale you would move to an IVF or HNSW index and shard by camera or time window — the retrieval layer is already abstracted behind get_clip_index(). The honest gap is ingestion, not search: we index at roughly 2 keyframes/second of footage on CPU, so real-time coverage of hundreds of cameras needs GPU workers, not a different algorithm.

questions.q: Why keyframes and not every frame?
questions.a: Keyframe sampling at ~2 fps. Every frame would multiply the index ~15× for almost no recall gain, since consecutive frames are near-identical — that is the same redundancy the grouping toggle exists to hide. The cost is that fast-moving objects can be missed between keyframes, which is exactly what the Scene Analytics quality badge reports per camera.

questions.q: Is any of this fabricated or pre-seeded for the demo?
questions.a: The footage is real stock CCTV-style video ingested through the same pipeline a station would use; the searches run live against FAISS at request time. Nothing on this screen is pre-computed for the demo — you can type an arbitrary query and watch it return in under 100 ms. What is not real is the case metadata elsewhere in the platform, which is seeded.

broken: DEMO-CRITICAL — thumbnails are rate-limited and result grids render as black boxes. /thumbnails/ falls into the same 120 req/min default bucket as the API. Measured: 150 sequential thumbnail requests → first HTTP 429 at request #114. In the browser, a 10-card grid had 9 of 10 thumbnails 429'd and a 60-card grid had 53 of 60 broken — bounding boxes floating on empty black cards. Root cause chain: (1) RateLimitMiddleware._classify in backend/app/security_mw.py sends anything that isn't /auth/login, /api/videos POST, /api/search/image|face or /api/admin/export/ to the 'default' 120/min bucket, which includes /thumbnails/; (2) it keys on request.client.host, which behind the nginx container is 172.20.0.3 for EVERY browser (confirmed in backend logs), even though nginx does set X-Real-IP; (3) one idle VisionScan tab already makes 66 API calls/min (measured over 60 s: health 20, videos 20, anomalies/summary 12, notifications 12, broadcasts 2). So a single presenter idling burns 55% of the budget, and one 60-card search finishes it off. Suggested one-line fix in _classify: return early with no limit when request.url.path.startswith('/thumbnails/'). Requires a backend restart, so I did not apply it. If you cannot restart: keep grouping ON (24 cards, not 60), avoid re-running searches rapidly, and close every other browser tab pointed at the app.

CLIP cannot do negation. "empty street with no people" returns 5 hits and every single one contains detected people (2, 1, 3, 1, 1). The often-repeated phrasing that it returns "the busiest scene" is an overstatement — the top hit has 2 people, while the crowded-market top hit has 7 — so do not say that on stage. The defensible line is: "CLIP has no NOT operator; every frame it returned still contains people." The sharper illustration if a judge pushes: per-object search for "no people" returns 60 hits led by stop signs and a fire hydrant.

"Find every object" hides the "Grouping moments" toggle and the state leaks across tabs. In frontend/src/components/SearchPanel.jsx the grouping toggle is rendered under {!perObject && (…)}, and switchMode() resets mode/file/group but never resets perObject. Consequence: enable "Find every object" on the Text tab, switch to the Object tab, and that tab now has ZERO toggles — the presenter cannot turn grouping on or off any more, with no indication why. Recovery is to switch back to Text and toggle per-object off. Avoid touching that toggle if you plan to move between tabs.

The report request has no user-facing error path. When POST /api/report was rate-limited, the UI threw an uncaught 'Request failed with status code 429' as a page error and the modal simply sat there — no toast, no message, no retry. On stage a throttled report looks like a hung button.

Camera scoping can return MORE hits than searching all 16 cameras. Per-object "red car" unscoped returns 24; scoped to CAM-12 it returns 38. That is because the relative relevance floor is 0.88 × the best score IN THE FILTERED SET — remove CAM-14's strong 0.3055 hit and the floor drops, letting weaker CAM-12 cars through. Defensible if explained, but do not show the two counts side by side without being ready for the question.
The camera rail is ordered by created_at DESC, so it reads CAM-16, 14, 15, 13, 12, 10, 11, 09, 08, 07, 04, 05, 06, 03, 01, 02 — scrambled to anyone expecting numeric order. Cosmetic only.

DO NOT click "Re-index" in the camera-feeds rail header. It POSTs /api/reindex, which queues a full pipeline re-run over all 16 ready videos as background tasks on a CPU-only backend. I did not click it and neither should the presenter.

questions.q: What happens when I type something YOLO has never heard of?
questions.a: The UI tries the exact label filter first. If that returns nothing, it automatically re-issues the query against the per-detection CLIP index — every detected object crop has its own embedding, 3,355 of them — and labels the result banner "not an exact object label — showing per-object visual matches (CLIP) instead". So "red car" works even though YOLO's 80 classes contain "car" but no colours.

questions.q: Why does grouping give 24 but ungrouped gives exactly 60? That looks like a round number.
questions.a: Good catch — 60 is a cap, not a total. The UI requests top_k=60 for per-object search. If you raise it, 78 crops pass the relevance filter and collapse to the same 24 tracked objects. So the honest statement is: 78 individual detections match, showing the first 60, which are 24 distinct physical objects.

questions.q: How do you know two detections are the same car rather than two cars?
questions.a: We do not guess from time or position — we use the track_id the tracker already assigned during ingestion, grouping on (video_id, label, track_id). That matters: two different red cars visible in the same second are two results, not one, which naive time-clustering would wrongly merge. Detections with no track_id are deliberately left ungrouped rather than lumped together, since we cannot know.

questions.q: That top hit is labelled "truck" but it is clearly a car. Is your detector wrong?
questions.a: Yes, on that instance. YOLO mislabels some vehicles in this footage, and we surface the label rather than hiding it. It matters less than it looks, because the per-object CLIP fallback ranks on the visual embedding of the crop, not on the label — that hit surfaced because the crop looks like a red car, regardless of what YOLO called it. The label chip is shown so the operator can see and discount the disagreement.

questions.q: Can this ever return nothing when nothing matches?
questions.a: The YOLO-label path can — an unused label returns zero. The per-object CLIP path effectively cannot, and that is a real weakness: the absolute floor is 0.22 but object crops sit at a higher noise floor, so "elephant in a swimming pool" still returns 13 cars and people. The whole-frame text path does return zero correctly. If a judge wants to see an honest empty result, use Text search, not this tab.

questions.q: Is the bounding box computed at search time or stored?
questions.a: Stored at ingestion, in the video's native pixel space, then converted to fractions of the frame at query time so the box lands correctly on a thumbnail scaled to a 480 px long edge. Rows from before that migration emit no box at all rather than a wrong one — a wrong box on evidence is worse than no box.

questions.q: Why is object search 30 ms but text search 80 ms?
questions.a: Object-label search never touches a model — it is an indexed SQL aggregate over the detections table. Text search has to embed the query string through CLIP's text encoder first. Per-object CLIP lands in between at 70 ms because it embeds the text once then does a FAISS lookup over 3,355 crop vectors.

questions.q: Is this just image hashing or a pixel diff?
questions.a: No — it is a CLIP image embedding, the same 512-d space the text queries land in. I proved it by feeding a probe that was cropped to 75%, downscaled to 320 px and re-encoded at JPEG quality 45; a hash would have missed entirely, and it still matched at 0.86. What it matches is scene composition and semantics, not bytes.

questions.q: Why did the red-car crop return nothing?
questions.a: Because this tab compares your image against WHOLE FRAMES, and a tight crop of one object has a completely different global composition from the wide street scene it came from. It scored 0.6887 against a 0.72 minimum. That threshold is deliberately high — for reference-image search a false positive is worse than an empty result. The right tool for an object crop is the per-object search on the Object tab, which compares crop-to-crop.

questions.q: Why is the threshold 0.72 here but 0.22 for text?
questions.a: Different modalities, different score distributions. Image-to-image CLIP similarity is naturally high — two unrelated street scenes already sit around 0.6 — so a meaningful match has to clear 0.72. Text-to-image similarity is compressed into a much lower band, where 0.3 is already a strong hit. Using one threshold for both would either flood the image results or silence the text results.

questions.q: What is the false positive rate?
questions.a: On the one probe I measured: zero. 22 hits returned, all 22 on the correct camera, none of the other 15 cameras or the remaining 395 indexed frames surfaced. That is a single-probe result on a 417-frame index, not a benchmark — I would not quote a general accuracy number from it.

questions.q: Could an officer upload a suspect's photo here instead of the Face tab?
questions.a: They could, and they should not. This tab embeds the whole image, so a portrait would match other portrait-like frames by composition rather than identity. Identity matching is the Suspect Face tab, which runs ArcFace on detected faces. I tested exactly this crossover: the face crop uploaded here returns 0 matches, which is the correct refusal.

questions.q: What model is doing the face matching, and why not CLIP?
questions.a: ArcFace, via InsightFace, run at ingestion over every detected face — 956 embeddings stored. CLIP is trained for semantic similarity and would happily match two different people who look alike in context; ArcFace is trained specifically for identity with an angular margin loss, so its embedding space separates individuals rather than scenes. They are stored in separate FAISS indexes and never mixed.

questions.q: 84% match — 84% of what? Is that a probability that it is the same person?
questions.a: No, and I would not let anyone read it that way. It is cosine similarity in ArcFace embedding space rendered as a percentage. Our accept threshold is 0.30. The honest interpretation is ranking plus a floor, not calibrated probability — we have not run a ROC on this dataset, so I cannot give you a false-accept rate. For a real deployment that calibration is mandatory before anyone acts on a match.

questions.q: How do you know these 13 hits are the same person and not 13 lookalikes?
questions.a: Strictly speaking I do not have ground-truth identity labels, so I can only give you the evidence: all 13 hits are on one camera within a 14-second window, and 262 indexed faces on the other cameras — including 87 on CAM-06 and 73 on CAM-12 — scored below threshold. That is consistent with one person walking through one frame. It is not proof, and the PDF report says as much on every page.

questions.q: This is face recognition on public CCTV. What stops it being abused?
questions.a: Three things, and I will be honest that they are the beginning rather than the end. The report footer stamps every exported PDF with a SHA-256 and the line "Frames are AI-ranked candidates and should be verified by an investigator before use as evidence" — the tool never asserts identity. The platform is role-gated so a citizen account cannot reach this screen. And the search is per-query and logged, not a standing watchlist. What is genuinely missing is a warrant/authorisation gate and a retention policy on the face index — I would not deploy this without both.

questions.q: Why is face search 560 ms when text is 80 ms?
questions.a: Because the probe has to be processed first: detect the face in the uploaded image, align it, then run the ArcFace encoder, before the FAISS lookup over 956 vectors even starts. The lookup itself is negligible. Text search only has to encode a short string.

questions.q: Only 956 faces from 417 frames — is the face detector missing people?
questions.a: It is finding what is findable. 694 of those 956 are on CAM-07, the close-range market camera; the overhead traffic cameras contribute almost none because faces are a handful of pixels at that distance and angle. That is an honest property of the camera geometry, not a tuning problem — CCTV mounted for vehicle coverage will not give you usable faces, which is why the Scene Analytics screen reports per-camera quality separately.

The matched thumbnail is a wide crowded-market frame in which the suspect is small and hard to see at card size. Unlike per-object search there is no bounding box drawn around the matched face, so from the audience it is not visually obvious what matched. Open the detail modal to make the point, or be ready to explain.

No calibrated confidence. The 0.30 accept threshold is a hand-set constant with no ROC or false-accept-rate analysis behind it on this dataset. If a judge asks for accuracy, say so plainly rather than quoting the 84% as an accuracy figure.

Only one identity was ever validated. All my testing used the single best probe; I have no evidence about how the system behaves on a harder face (profile, motion-blurred, partially occluded). Do not claim general face-recognition performance.

questions.q: What does "5.6× fewer once tracked" actually mean?
questions.a: CAM-07 has 251 person detections across its keyframes but only 45 distinct tracks. Every keyframe re-detects the same people, so the raw count massively overstates footfall — tracking links those boxes into one identity each. The 5.6× is the inflation factor you would have reported if you had naively counted detections. We show both numbers and the ratio precisely so nobody quotes the wrong one.

questions.q: Your own screen says CAM-12 tracking quality is "poor". Why should I trust the 95 objects it just counted?
questions.a: You should trust it less than the CAM-07 number, and that is exactly why the badge is there. Poor means 43% of detections were seen only once or twice, so the tracker is fragmenting one object into several — which inflates "distinct objects" upward. The direction of the error is knowable: on a poor-graded camera, distinct-object counts are an over-estimate and the true figure is lower. We would rather hand an investigator a graded number than a confident wrong one.

questions.q: How is the quality grade computed?
questions.a: Two inputs, both shown in the tooltip: keyframe density (fps estimate) and measured fragmentation — the share of detections belonging to tracks seen only once or twice. CAM-07 is good at ~2.0 fps and 13% fragmentation; CAM-01 is poor at ~0.2 fps and 100% fragmentation, because it only has 3 keyframes so every detection is its own track. It is a heuristic, not a learned metric, and it is deliberately pessimistic.

questions.q: Is the tripwire counting people or detections?
questions.a: Tracks. A crossing is registered when a track's bottom-centre point moves from one side of the line to the other, so one person walking through counts once regardless of how many keyframes they appear in. The event list names the track ID, which is why you see the same #11 cross out and then back in — that is one person doubling back, not two people.

questions.q: Why does the crossing count change so much when I move the line?
questions.a: Because it only counts tracks that actually cross that line, and the footage has strong movement corridors. On CAM-10 a line at 30% height catches 31 crossings; the same line at 60% catches 9. That is real geometry, not instability — but it does mean an operator has to place the line where the traffic is, which is why the tool is interactive rather than automatic.

questions.q: What makes the PDF forensically useful rather than just a printout?
questions.a: Four things. Every frame carries its camera, timestamp, frame ID and source filename, so it is traceable back to the original video. The object inventory per frame is recorded. The footer carries a SHA-256 of the document content, rendered two-pass so the hash is reproducible — re-render the same content and you get the same digest, which means tampering is detectable. And the footer states that frames are AI-ranked candidates requiring investigator verification, so the document never overstates itself.

questions.q: Can I verify that hash independently?
questions.a: Yes in principle and with one caveat you should know about. The two-pass render pins the timestamp and turns on ReportLab's invariant flag, so identical content plus identical timestamp produces byte-identical output — I confirmed that by generating the same report twice and getting the same digest. The caveat is that the documented X-Integrity-SHA256 response header is not currently emitted by the endpoint, so today you verify against the value printed in the footer rather than against a header.

questions.q: Is the report linked to a case, or is it a loose file?
questions.a: The report modal has a "Link to one of your cases" dropdown populated with the officer's live cases, so the export can be filed against case #29, #35 and so on rather than floating free. And from the search results, "Draft FIR in Arbiter" carries the camera, timestamp and hit count into the FIR drafting module. The CCTV search is a step in the case workflow, not a separate tool.

broken: /api/videos/{id}/zone-analytics and /api/videos/{id}/line-crossings have no auth dependency at all. Every other VisionScan route takes Depends(auth_gate); these two in backend/app/api/zone_routes.py take none. Confirmed by calling both with no token and getting HTTP 200. This is invisible today because VISIONSCAN_REQUIRE_AUTH=false, but flipping that flag to true would secure every route EXCEPT these two. Worth fixing after the demo, not before.

The X-Integrity-SHA256 response header is never sent. build_report_with_integrity() returns the digest and integrity_headers() exists to serve it, but /api/report calls the plain build_report() and sets only Content-Disposition — the function has no caller outside report.py. The hash is still stamped in the PDF footer, so the feature works, but do not claim the API exposes it.

A report requested with nonexistent frame IDs returns HTTP 200 and a PDF that says "Frames in report: 1" while rendering no frames, because the count is len(frame_ids) rather than the number actually resolved. Cosmetic, but it is a forensic document making a false count claim.

PDF timestamps are in the container's clock/timezone, not IST. My reports generated just after midnight IST on 20 Aug are stamped "2026-08-19 19:53:48". For an evidence document the timezone matters; a judge reading the date could reasonably query it.
Zone analytics for a nonexistent video ID returns HTTP 200 with empty results instead of 404 (tracks endpoint correctly returns 404). Minor inconsistency.

The report request has no user-facing error handling. When it was rate-limited the UI threw an uncaught 'Request failed with status code 429' page error and the modal simply hung — no message, no retry. If the PDF button appears dead on stage, that is why; wait 30 seconds and click again.
DO NOT click "Re-index" in the Camera Feeds header. It queues a full re-ingestion of all 16 videos on a CPU-only backend and would disrupt everything mid-demo.
"1.0× fewer once tracked" on CAM-01 is a confusing way to say "no compression at all". Minor copy issue on a screen you may deliberately show.

Thumbnail rate-limiting affects the Scene Analytics drawing canvas too — it loads one keyframe, which can 429 and leave the dashed "frame unavailable" placeholder, making the zone/line tools undrawable. If that happens, close and reopen the panel after ~30 seconds. Full root-cause analysis on the Text search page.

questions.q: Is this real translation or machine output with English fallback?
questions.a: Real, and checkable. There are 853 keys in each of en/hi/gu with zero missing and zero extra — I enumerated every one of the 16 section files and diffed them. Exactly three strings are byte-identical across all three languages: UPI, SMS and WhatsApp, which are brand names. There IS an English fallback in the lookup chain (active language → English → the key itself) but nothing is currently reaching it.

questions.q: Why is the CCTV search box English-only when the rest of the UI is trilingual?
questions.a: Because CLIP's text encoder is trained on English. We embed the query into the same vector space as the frames, so a Devanagari query lands in a meaningless region. I measured it: 'red car' returns one hit on CAM-14, the actual red-car camera; 'लाल कार' returns 8 hits at ~27% topped by CAM-09, which is pedestrians. Rather than hide that, the Hindi placeholder literally says 'अंग्रेज़ी में लिखें' — write in English. Fixing it properly means swapping in a multilingual CLIP variant or putting an IndicTrans layer in front of the encoder; both are real options, neither is done.

questions.q: Is the language a browser setting or does it follow the officer?
questions.a: It follows the officer. setLang writes to localStorage AND fires PATCH /api/auth/me/preferences, which persists language on the users row. I verified the whole loop: set Hindi, sign out, sign back in — still Hindi; then sign in as the citizen on the same browser and it comes up English, because that is the citizen's stored value. localStorage is used for exactly one thing: rendering the login screen in the last-used language before anyone has authenticated.

questions.q: Show me a string that is still English when it shouldn't be.
questions.a: Several, and they cluster on the VisionScan screen. The results header renders '1 matches for red car' in English — and the annoying part is that the translation key vision.matchesFor exists and IS translated in both languages; App.jsx:470 just hardcodes the word. Same story for the 'Find every object' button at App.jsx:510, where the identical key is used correctly two lines above. Plus all 16 camera tiles show 'Ready' because utils.js statusBadge() hardcodes the four status labels, and role badges show raw admin/lead/officer/citizen because enums.js has no role_* keys. None of these break anything; they are five or six one-line wiring misses, not missing translation work.

questions.q: Why not use react-i18next?
questions.a: Deliberate — there's a comment about it in the module. Three fixed languages, static strings, simple {placeholder} substitution: a React context plus three plain objects does it in about 80 lines instead of a 40KB dependency and its plugin chain. Nothing outside i18n/index.jsx knows how lookup works, so swapping in a real library later is a contained change. The trade-off they accepted is no plurals — which is exactly why you see '1 matches' instead of '1 match'.

questions.q: What happens to a language that isn't one of the three?
questions.a: The API rejects it: PATCH with {"language":"fr"} returns 400 'language must be one of en|hi|gu'. Client-side, setLang no-ops if the code isn't in the dictionary map. And any key that somehow missed a translation degrades to readable English rather than showing a raw key or a blank cell.

questions.q: Do the AI-generated outputs (Arbiter FIR drafts, CrimeGPT documents) get translated too?
questions.a: No, and that's a different problem from UI strings. The Arbiter statute corpus is IPC / IT Act 2000 / CrPC in English, and CrimeGPT's document generator takes a language argument separately. The UI chrome around them is fully Hindi/Gujarati; the legal text is not, because a machine-translated statute reference in a police document would be a liability rather than a feature.

questions.q: If the app crashes, is the error screen translated?
questions.a: No — 'Something went wrong' and 'Reload' are English-only. It's a class component, so it can't use the useT hook, and arguably you don't want the crash handler depending on the i18n context that may be the thing that broke. Honest answer: it's defensible, but it means a Hindi demo that hits an error shows an English wall.

This is the single most-looked-at line on the VisionScan screen.

PLURALISATION: '1 matches for …' and '1 frames selected' — the hand-rolled i18n has no plural support. Cosmetic, but a judge reading the screen will notice.

SILENT SAVE FAILURE: setLang fires updatePreferences as fire-and-forget with .catch(() => {}) (frontend/src/i18n/index.jsx:55). When the API was rate-limited during my testing the PATCH was rejected and the language silently reverted on next login, with no indication to the user. Single-presenter demo won't hit this; two people testing simultaneously did.

SHARED-ACCOUNT GOTCHA: language is per USER, so if two people are signed into admin@city.gov at once they will fight over the setting — I watched it flip back to English mid-test because another session changed it. Make sure nobody else is logged in as admin during the demo. I have reset all four demo accounts to English.

There is no language switcher ON the login screen — it inherits the last language this browser used. If the demo laptop was last used in Gujarati, the sign-in page opens in Gujarati and there is no control to change it until after sign-in.

name: Citizen portal — public-facing complaint flow
route: Sign in as citizen@example.com / citizen123 → lands directly on Complaints ("My Complaints"). Nav is only Legal Feed / Cases / Complaints.
one_liner: A public complaint front-door with a cyber-fraud-specific form, live status and police reply visible to the reporter, a deep link into their own case, and a star rating once it closes — with the police-internal half of the platform enforced away at the API, not just hidden in the nav.

headline.what: Tick 'Cybercrime' and the form transforms into a fraud intake: 10 named fraud types, 8 fraud channels, amount lost in ₹, and 'Hours ago?'. Enter a low number of hours and a red banner appears: 'Golden hour: call 1930 immediately — fraudulent transfers may still be freezable.'
headline.why_impressive: This is domain knowledge, not a generic form. The 1930 golden-hour window is the actual thing that decides whether a victim's money is recoverable, and the product nudges the citizen toward it at the exact moment they are typing the amount they lost.
headline.exact_steps: Complaints → tick 'Cybercrime' → Fraud type 'UPI / OTP Fraud' → Amount lost 47500 → Hours ago 3 → the golden-hour banner appears above Submit.

headline.what: Submit and the complaint appears instantly at the top of the citizen's own list with a live status chip — Submitted → Under review → Assigned → Converted — and, where police have replied, the reply text inline: 'Police response: FIR registered; 1930 freeze request raised with the bank nodal officer.'
headline.why_impressive: Closes the loop that is missing from almost every real government complaint portal. The citizen sees the same status the station sees, plus the actual words the officer wrote, without a phone call.
headline.exact_steps: Fill the form → Submit complaint → your complaint is row 1 with a 'Submitted' chip. Scroll one row down to the seeded 'Online fraud reported' to show a 'Converted' complaint with a police response and a 'View case #38' button.

headline.what: Click 'View case #38' and the citizen is inside their own case — status Closed, severity Critical, and the verdict: 'Amount frozen at the beneficiary bank and refunded; chargesheet filed under BNS 318(4) and IT Act 66D.' Then five stars: 'Rate your experience'.
headline.why_impressive: A citizen-facing outcome with a real legal disposition, and a feedback loop that feeds the station's own dashboard — the Command Dashboard shows AVG RATING 4.17/5 from 6 ratings, which is the citizens' score of the police, computed from this exact widget.
headline.exact_steps: On the 'Converted' complaint click 'View case #38' → read the verdict → click the 4th star → 'Thanks for rating (4★).' → switch to admin and show AVG RATING on the Dashboard.

headline.what: The citizen sees 6 of the 10 cases. The other 4 are not merely hidden — requesting them directly returns 403, and their evidence returns 403.
headline.why_impressive: The answer to the obvious security question is a status code, not a screenshot. Visibility is a per-case citizen_visible flag enforced server-side; the nav hiding is cosmetic on top of a real boundary.
headline.exact_steps: If challenged: a citizen token on GET /api/cases/29 returns 403, /api/cases/29/evidence returns 403, and /api/analytics/summary, /api/analytics/map, /api/anomalies and /api/predict/risk all return 403.

questions.q: How do you stop a citizen from seeing police-internal case data?
questions.a: Two layers, and the one that matters is server-side. Cases carry a citizen_visible flag; the citizen sees 6 of 10 and a direct GET on any of the other 4 returns 403, as does their evidence. Staff analytics — /analytics/summary, /analytics/map, /anomalies, /predict/risk — all return 403 for a citizen token. Inside a case they can see, they get two tabs (Evidence, Messages) instead of the staff set, and evidence is gated per item: case #38 has 1 evidence record and the citizen sees 'No evidence visible.' Hiding the nav is just cosmetics on top of that.

questions.q: Your demo citizen sees 2002 complaints. Isn't that a data leak?
questions.a: Fair challenge, and I chased it. It is a seeding artefact, not a leak: the synthetic seed attributed all 2002 complaints to citizen_id 20, which is the demo citizen, so they genuinely are the reporter of every one. I proved the filter works by registering a second citizen — that account saw 0 complaints, filed one, then saw exactly 1. Scoping is correct; the demo account is just an unusually prolific victim.

questions.q: What is the 'golden hour' banner actually doing?
questions.a: It's a client-side rule on the 'Hours ago?' field. If the fraud is recent it surfaces the 1930 advisory, because within that window the transfer can often still be frozen at the beneficiary bank. It's a prompt, not an integration — we are not calling 1930 or the bank. The seeded case verdict shows what the follow-through looks like when a station does act on it: 'Amount frozen at the beneficiary bank and refunded.'

questions.q: Can a citizen rate any case, or spam ratings?
questions.a: The widget only renders for a non-staff user on a case with status 'closed' that is visible to them, and POST /cases/{id}/rate is scoped to that. What I would flag honestly: the client calls rateCase with .catch(() => {}) and then unconditionally shows 'Thanks for rating' — so if the write ever failed the citizen would be told it succeeded. I did not find a duplicate-rating guard on the client either.

questions.q: Why can a citizen list all 16 CCTV feeds?
questions.a: That's the weakest point I found on this screen. GET /api/videos returns 200 for a citizen token with camera IDs, filenames, fps, durations and keyframe counts. It is metadata only — no frames, no thumbnails, no search, and the frame and search endpoints are gated — but a citizen learning that CAM-14 is 'traffic_redcar_06.mp4' is more than they need. It reads like the video routes predate the platform's RBAC layer and were never brought under it.

questions.q: Does the citizen see the officer's real name and notes?
questions.a: No. They see the case status, severity, priority, a member count, and the verdict text an officer wrote when closing. Investigation notes, documents, the timeline and the schedule are staff-only tabs that are not rendered for them, and evidence is per-item gated. The 'Police response' on the complaint is a field an officer deliberately fills during triage — it's meant to be read by the citizen.

questions.q: What happens between 'Submitted' and a case existing?
questions.a: A lead or admin opens the complaint in the staff inbox and triages it: sets severity and priority, writes the response message the citizen will see, and ticks 'Open a case'. That converts the complaint (status becomes 'Converted'), creates the case, and the citizen's complaint card grows a 'View case #N' button. All four statuses — Submitted, Under review, Assigned, Converted — are visible to the citizen throughout.

questions.q: Is the complaint form validated on the server or just the browser?
questions.a: Both, but not symmetrically. Title and description are HTML5-required in the browser, and the server rejects malformed payloads with a 422. The uncomfortable part is what the front end does with a 422 — see the login page notes; the same array-shaped error body that crashes the registration form would crash other screens too. The complaint submit path itself does not use that error-rendering pattern, so it is safe.

broken: GET /api/videos returns 200 for a citizen token, exposing all 16 camera IDs, source filenames, fps, durations and keyframe counts. Metadata only — frames and search are gated — but it is not access-controlled the way the analytics endpoints are.

Rating is a silent-success path: CaseWorkspace.jsx:348 calls API.rateCase(...).catch(() => {}) and then unconditionally sets done, so a failed write still shows 'Thanks for rating (N★).' There is also no visible guard against rating the same case twice from the UI.

The staff complaint inbox renders all 2002 complaints in one list — 29,022 DOM nodes and 1,993 'Triage' buttons, no pagination, no search, no filter. It renders in 1.7s and uses 17.4 MB of heap so it is not broken, but do not scroll it looking for a specific complaint on stage; you will scroll for a long time.
The citizen case header shows '· 1 member(s)' — the size of the investigating team. Harmless but it is internal staffing information appearing on a citizen-facing screen.

Complaint titles and descriptions in the seeded data are English only; the categories, statuses and severities around them translate. In a Hindi or Gujarati demo the complaint cards therefore look half-translated. That is seed data, not an i18n bug, but it looks like one.

Registering a new citizen with a password shorter than 6 characters crashes the entire app to the error screen — see the Login page for the full write-up. It is reachable from the citizen portal's own 'New citizen? Register' link, so it belongs on this page's do-not-touch list too.

name: PDF investigation reports — VisionScan report export
route: Sign in as staff → VisionScan → run a search → tick the checkbox on the frames you want → floating tray at the bottom → 'Generate Report' → optionally link a case → 'Download PDF'
one_liner: A one-click forensic PDF that turns selected CCTV search hits into a branded, chain-of-custody-stamped investigation report — SHA-256 sealed via a deterministic two-pass render, in under a quarter of a second.

headline.what: Tick frames from a live search and a floating tray appears; two clicks later a branded 'CCTV Investigation Report' PDF downloads. 10 frames → 2 pages, 538.7 KB, in 0.21 seconds.
headline.why_impressive: The gap between 'the AI found something' and 'I have a document I can put in a case file' is where most demos stop. This closes it in two clicks, and the speed means you can do it live without dead air.
headline.exact_steps: VisionScan → search 'red car' → click 'Find every object' (24 results) → tick 10 checkboxes → 'Generate Report' → 'Download PDF'.

headline.what: Every page footer carries 'Integrity SHA-256: 7589…8585 · generated 2026-08-19 20:13:02' plus 'CONFIDENTIAL — For authorized investigation use only'. The hash comes from a two-pass render: pass 1 hashes the content, pass 2 re-renders with that hash stamped into the footer.
headline.why_impressive: Naive self-hashing is impossible — stamping the hash changes the bytes. The two-pass trick with ReportLab's invariant flag (which pins internal PDF timestamps and IDs) makes the document bytes a pure function of its content, so the printed hash is genuinely re-verifiable. I proved it: two identical requests produced byte-identical 165,781-byte PDFs with the same digest.
headline.exact_steps: Open the PDF → scroll to any page footer → read the Integrity line. If a judge pushes, mention it's a two-pass render with rl_config.invariant = 1.

headline.what: Per frame, the report prints the provenance a court would ask for: 'CAM-14 @ 00:00:16', 'Frame #2236 · traffic_redcar_06.mp4', and the full YOLO object inventory 'Objects: car(16), person(3), truck(2), motorcycle(1)'.
headline.why_impressive: It ties every thumbnail back to a specific camera, a specific timecode, a specific source file and a specific frame index — and it publishes what the detector saw, not just what the operator was looking for. That is auditable.
headline.exact_steps: Point at any thumbnail caption block in the PDF.

headline.what: The dialog offers your open cases and auto-titles the report from the one you pick — selecting '#29 · Digital-arrest cyber-fraud ring busted' fills the title as 'Case #29 · Digital-arrest cyber-fraud ring busted', which also becomes the PDF's document title metadata.
headline.why_impressive: The report is filed against real casework rather than being an orphan download, and the investigator field pre-fills with the signed-in officer's name and badge number — 'Station Admin (ADM-001)'.
headline.exact_steps: In the Generate Report dialog, open the 'Link case' dropdown and pick #29 — watch the title field fill itself.

headline.what: The report ends with an honest disclaimer: 'Frames are AI-ranked candidates and should be verified by an investigator before use as evidence.'
headline.why_impressive: It is the sentence that makes the whole thing deployable. The team is claiming a search tool that narrows 417 indexed frames to 10, not an oracle that decides guilt — and they put that in writing on the artefact itself.
headline.exact_steps: Scroll to the last line of the final page.

questions.q: What does the SHA-256 in the footer actually protect against?
questions.a: Alteration of an issued document. It is a two-pass render: pass 1 builds the PDF with a blank stamp and hashes those bytes, pass 2 rebuilds the same content with that digest printed in the footer. ReportLab runs with rl_config.invariant = 1 so internal PDF timestamps and object IDs are pinned, which makes the byte stream a pure function of the content — I verified two identical requests produce byte-identical files. Be precise about the claim though: the 'Generated' timestamp is part of the hashed content, so re-rendering the same frames three seconds later gives a different hash. It seals a specific issued document; it is not a content-only fingerprint of the frames.

questions.q: Could someone regenerate the PDF, change a frame, and re-stamp a matching hash?
questions.a: Yes, if they control the server — the hash is self-computed, not signed by an external authority. This is tamper-evidence, not non-repudiation. Making it non-repudiable means signing the digest with a key the station doesn't hold, or anchoring it to an external timestamp authority. Neither is implemented. What it does buy you is that a PDF edited after download will no longer match its own footer.

questions.q: Are the AI's bounding boxes in the report?
questions.a: No, and I'd rather say so than get caught. On screen the green box is a CSS overlay positioned from normalised coordinates the API returns as match_bbox — that's why the on-screen result looks so precise. The PDF embeds the raw keyframe, so the box isn't there. What the PDF does carry instead is the full YOLO object inventory per frame in text — 'Objects: car(16), person(3), truck(2), motorcycle(1)' — so the detection evidence is present, just not drawn.

questions.q: Why is the PDF creation date the year 2000?
questions.a: That's ReportLab's invariant mode, and it's deliberate. Fixed internal timestamps are exactly what makes the byte output reproducible and therefore the integrity hash verifiable. The real generation time is printed in the document body and in every page footer. It does look odd in File > Properties, and while we were in there we also left author and subject as '(anonymous)' / '(unspecified)' even though we know the investigator's name — that's a genuine miss, one line to fix.

questions.q: You mention an X-Integrity-SHA256 header — I don't see it.
questions.a: You're right, it isn't emitted. The report service defines build_report_with_integrity() returning (bytes, digest) and an integrity_headers() helper specifically for this, but the route at backend/app/api/routes.py:393 still calls the older build_report(), which returns bytes only. So the footer stamp is correct and the machine-readable header is missing. It's a two-line fix at the serving site that nobody made after the integrity work landed.

questions.q: How big does this get with a realistic number of frames?
questions.a: Roughly linear at about 50 KB per embedded keyframe: 1 frame is 51,816 bytes on one page, 10 frames is 551,641 bytes on two pages, six thumbnails to a page. So a 50-frame report would be around 2.5 MB and 9 pages. Generation is fast enough not to matter — 0.04s for one frame, 0.21s for ten — because the keyframes are already extracted and on disk; the report step is layout, not inference.

questions.q: What happens if the PDF fails to generate during the demo?
questions.a: Nothing visible, which is the problem. App.jsx:255 has no catch and ReportTray's generate() uses try/finally without one, so a rejected request just stops the spinner and leaves the dialog open with no message. The presenter would be standing there clicking a button that appears to do nothing. Everything I ran returned 200, but that's the failure mode if it happens.

questions.q: Can a citizen generate one of these?
questions.a: The button lives inside VisionScan, which citizens have no nav entry for, and the search and frame endpoints are staff-gated. I did not find a way to reach the report dialog as a citizen. I'd note the /report route itself sits behind a general auth gate rather than an explicit staff-role check, so I would want that tightened before this went anywhere near production.

questions.q: Why does the report timestamp not match the clock in the room?
questions.a: Container clock skew — the backend is on UTC and the demo is in IST. When my host clock read 01:43 the report stamped 20:13 the previous day, a 5h30m difference. On a chain-of-custody document that is worth fixing before anyone deploys it, because 'generated at' on an evidence artefact should match the wall clock of the station that generated it.

broken: The green bounding box is NOT in the PDF. It is a CSS overlay in FrameCard.jsx drawn from match_bbox; the report embeds the raw keyframe. Do not tell judges the box is in the report — show the box on screen and the object inventory in the PDF.

Clock skew: the container is on UTC while the presenter is on IST, so the report's 'Generated' line is 5h30m behind the room. Measured: PDF stamped 2026-08-19 20:13:02 while the host clock read 2026-08-20 01:43. On a chain-of-custody document a judge may well ask about this.

questions.q: Why do a wrong password and an unknown email give the same error?
questions.a: Deliberate anti-enumeration. If the messages differed, the login form becomes an oracle for discovering which email addresses have accounts — useful for targeting officers with phishing. The same rule is applied to the forgot-password flow, which returns 'If the email exists, a reset token was sent' regardless. Both responses come back on the same path in comparable time, around 2.5 seconds.

questions.q: You're showing real passwords on the login screen. Isn't that a problem?
questions.a: Yes, and it's gated for exactly that reason — the panel is dev-only demo seeding, and the seed module is explicit that these are DEV ONLY credentials controlled by a settings.seed_demo_users flag. It exists so judges can drive four roles without waiting on us. For any real deployment the flag is off, the accounts don't exist, and the panel doesn't render. I'd want to see that verified in the deployment checklist rather than take it on trust.

questions.q: How are sessions handled — JWT, cookies, refresh tokens?
questions.a: A bearer JWT in localStorage, injected by an axios request interceptor. The payload carries sub, role, an exp and a tv field — token_version — which is the revocation mechanism: bump the user's token_version and every outstanding token for them stops validating. There is no refresh token; when the JWT expires you sign in again. A response interceptor drops the token and reloads on a 401, deliberately excluding the login call itself so a wrong password doesn't cause a reload loop.

questions.q: What stops someone brute-forcing these logins?
questions.a: A token-bucket rate limiter keyed on (IP, route class): 10 requests per minute for auth routes, 120 for the general API, 20 for uploads, with a Retry-After header on the 429. Worth flagging for tomorrow specifically — it's per IP, so if several judges try the demo accounts from the same conference wifi behind one NAT, they share the 10/min budget and will start getting locked out. If more than two people will be logging in at once, that number wants raising before the session.

questions.q: What is the single worst bug on this screen?
questions.a: Registering with a password shorter than six characters white-screens the entire application. The server correctly returns 422, but FastAPI's 422 body puts detail as an ARRAY of validation objects, and the client does setError(err?.response?.data?.detail || ...) and renders it — React refuses to render an object as a child and throws error #31, which unmounts everything to the ErrorBoundary. Only a Reload button remains. The same pattern exists at 15 call sites, and I confirmed a second demo-reachable one: Admin → Add staff user with a short password crashes identically. The root-cause fix is two lines in the axios response interceptor that already exists in frontend/src/api.js — normalise an array-shaped detail into a string once, and all 15 sites are fixed. I did not apply it because other agents are testing this stack and it needs a frontend rebuild.

questions.q: Can I reset a password with no mail server?
questions.a: Yes, that's what the 'Offline demo' wording is about. Forgot password generates a token; instead of relying on SMTP it tells you to read it from the admin outbox or the server log, then paste it into the 'Have a token?' form. The whole platform is built to run air-gapped — same reasoning as Arbiter's offline mode and the bundled legal corpus — so the auth flows had to work without outbound mail too.

questions.q: Is the login screen translated?
questions.a: Yes, and it's done cleverly: it reads the last language this browser used out of localStorage, so if an officer was working in Hindi and signs out, the sign-in page is already Hindi before anyone authenticates. The gap is that there's no language switcher ON the login screen — if the laptop was last used in Gujarati, a judge can't change it until after signing in.

questions.q: What happens if the backend is slow or momentarily unreachable?
questions.a: Worse than it should. The session bootstrap at auth.jsx:16-18 is API.authMe().then(setUser).catch(() => API.setToken(null)) — the catch is unconditional, so ANY failure, including a 429 or a transient network blip, throws away a perfectly valid token and drops the user back to the login screen. It should only clear on a 401. I hit this repeatedly while the API was rate-limited during testing: reload the page at the wrong moment and you're logged out. One-line fix, but it's a real risk if the demo box gets busy.

questions.q: Are there security headers, or is this a bare dev server?
questions.a: They're there — x-content-type-options, x-frame-options, referrer-policy, permissions-policy and a content-security-policy on API responses, applied by a middleware that sits outermost specifically so the headers are stamped even on 429 and 423 short-circuits. Passwords are hashed, never stored plaintext.

broken: CRITICAL — DO NOT DEMO: registering with a password shorter than 6 characters crashes the ENTIRE app to a white 'Something went wrong / Minified React error #31' screen with only a 'Reload' button. Reproduced 100% of the time. Root cause: FastAPI returns 422 with detail as an ARRAY of objects; frontend/src/components/platform/LoginView.jsx:36 does setError(err?.response?.data?.detail || …) and renders the array, which React refuses. FIX (2 lines, in the interceptor that already exists at frontend/src/api.js:21-31): if Array.isArray(err?.response?.data?.detail) replace it with detail.map(e => e.msg).join('; '). That one change fixes all 15 call sites.

SAME CRASH, second demo-reachable path: Admin → Add staff user with a password under 6 characters crashes identically (confirmed, HTTP 422 on /api/users). If you demo user management, always type a 6+ character temp password.

13 more call sites share the crash pattern and are one bad 422 away from the same white screen: App.jsx:173, ArbiterPanel.jsx:66, GovIntelPanel.jsx:115/138/204/222, AdminView.jsx:122/471/654, AnalyticsView.jsx:47, CaseWorkspace.jsx:190/221, SceneAnalytics.jsx:81/117.

frontend/src/auth.jsx:16-18 — API.authMe().then(setUser).catch(() => API.setToken(null)) discards the auth token on ANY error, not just a 401. A 429 or a momentary network blip on page reload silently logs the user out. I hit this repeatedly under load. Fix: only clear the token when e?.response?.status === 401.

Login rate limit is 10 requests/minute per IP. Several judges signing in from the same NAT'd conference wifi will share that budget and start seeing 429s. Consider raising rate_limit_login_per_min in backend/app/config.py:159 before the session if more than two people will log in concurrently.

No language switcher on the login screen. It inherits the browser's last-used language from localStorage with no way to change it until after sign-in — so if the laptop was last driven in Gujarati, the sign-in page opens in Gujarati.
The ErrorBoundary crash screen is English-only ('Something went wrong', 'Reload') — it is a class component and cannot use the i18n hook. So a Hindi demo that hits any crash shows an English wall.

Demo credentials for all four accounts are printed in plaintext on the login screen. It is flag-gated dev seeding and correct for the demo, but confirm the flag is off in any deployed build before this is shown to anyone outside the room.

questions.q: Did anything 404 or throw?

questions.q: What happens when the backend can't keep up?
questions.a: That's where the sharp edges are. There's a token-bucket limiter at 120 requests/min per IP for general API calls, and during testing several agents were driving the same box, so I got to watch the degraded path. It's not broken — 1.7 seconds to render, 17.4 MB of heap — but there's no pagination, no search and no filter, so finding a specific complaint means scrolling. Don't go looking for one live; open it, show the top few rows, and move on.

questions.q: Is the empty Live Alerts screen a failure?

Anomaly Watch runs a hybrid CLIP+YOLO detector over the feeds for fire, smoke, accidents, weapons and violence, and pins incidents the moment they're seen. With the seeded clips there's nothing currently active, so it correctly says 'All clear — no active alerts.' The filters and the explanation are still there. An empty alerts board in a policing product is the good outcome.

questions.q: Is the Hindi a machine translation done at request time?
questions.a: No — it is a static per-language message catalogue shipped with the build, so it costs nothing at runtime and works offline. The switch is a per-user preference stored on the user record, which is why it survives a reload and why two officers on the same station can run the console in different languages.

questions.q: Everything is translated except the place names. Why?
questions.a: Because they are identifiers, not copy. Locality names, camera IDs, filenames and frame IDs get quoted into evidence and into the PDF report; translating them would break the link back to the source. Separately, the CLIP search queries must stay in English because the embedding model is English-trained — translating a query would silently degrade retrieval. So the rule is: interface translates, evidence and model inputs do not.

questions.q: So can an officer type a search query in Hindi?
questions.a: They can type it, but they should not expect good results — CLIP's text encoder is English-trained and a Devanagari query lands in a poorly-populated region of the embedding space. That is a known ceiling, not something the language switch fixes. The same limitation shows up in the PDF documents, where Indic body text is a separate unsolved problem in the renderer.

questions.q: Does the notification bell push, or poll?
questions.a: Polls, every 5 seconds, alongside the anomaly-summary poller. That polling is also part of why the shared rate-limit bucket drains so fast — the bell and the ticker together are two of the six background pollers running on every open tab.

broken: The notification panel closes ONLY by clicking the bell a second time. Escape does not close it and clicking outside does not close it — verified. Worse, it stays open across a module change, so it will hang over the top-right corner of the next screen the presenter navigates to. If it is covering something, click the bell again.

Opening the bell marks everything read and the red count badge is gone for good. I burned the admin account's badge doing this test, so the admin bell now shows no unread count. If the presenter wants a red badge visible on stage, do not open the bell beforehand — or use the citizen account, which still has unread items.

The admin bell's three notifications are all QA artefacts: 'New complaint filed: QA probe scope test', 'New complaint filed: QA UPI OTP fraud 013203', and '[MEDIUM] QA test advisory — ignore: Pre-demo check of the broadcast pipeline.' If a judge asks to see the bell on the admin account, that is what they will read. The citizen bell is clean and much better.
The alert ticker is permanently grey because there are zero anomaly events. It is not broken, but do not point at it expecting a red pulse.

questions.q: Everything you have shown is pre-ingested footage. Can it watch a live camera?
questions.a: Yes, and the control is on this screen — the Live Feed tab takes an RTSP, HLS or YouTube-live URL and there are two modes: capture a bounded window, or go live and index continuously while you watch and search the same stream. We ship three intentionally-public streams so it demonstrates itself out of the box. I have verified all three are reachable from inside the backend container right now. What we have not done is point it at a real Gujarat traffic camera — that is a URL, not an engineering change.

questions.q: What stops someone pointing this at a private camera?
questions.a: Three things, and the first is a policy statement printed on the panel itself rather than buried in docs. Technically, a non-admin caller goes through a public-address assertion on the URL before anything is stored, and because a YouTube link can resolve to a private address, the resolved stream URL is re-validated inside the worker as well. An authenticated admin is trusted to ingest an internal LAN feed, which is the correct behaviour for a station operating its own cameras. What we do not have is a warrant or authorisation gate — that is a real gap for deployment.

questions.q: If you go live, does the anomaly watch fire?
questions.a: That is exactly the difference. The auto-case and dispatch loop is gated on the feed being LIVE — uploads of historical footage deliberately never notify or auto-create a case, so reviewing old evidence cannot spam the control room. All 16 seeded feeds are is_live=false, which is why Live Alerts is empty. A live feed is the only way to demonstrate the full detection→case→dispatch loop on this data.

questions.q: Why do the cameras have such different keyframe counts?
questions.a: Because keyframes are sampled at roughly 2 fps against clip length and content, and the source clips differ. CAM-12 is 28 seconds and yields 60 keyframes; CAM-01 is 13 seconds and yields only 3, which is exactly why Scene Analytics grades CAM-01 'poor' with 100% track fragmentation. The rail shows the raw budget so the quality grade downstream is not a surprise.

broken: "Delete feed" sits on every one of the 16 camera cards, always visible, directly beside the "Scene analytics" button the presenter is expected to click repeatedly during the demo. I found no confirmation step. One slip removes a camera from the demo. This is the highest-probability destructive misclick in the product and it was not in the coverage document at all.

Going live or capturing once BOTH insert a new videos row before any processing, so either one permanently makes it 17 feeds. That collides head-on with the dashboard headline "16 camera feeds, 417 indexed frames" and with the Live Alerts recommendation to ingest a fire clip. You can have at most ONE of: round dashboard numbers, a live-stream demo, or a populated Live Alerts screen. Decide before 9am, not on stage.

The three catalogued live feeds are public INTERNET URLs (mux.dev, unified-streaming.com, akamaihd.net). They resolve tonight from both the host and the container, but if the venue Wi-Fi is captive-portalled or blocked, clicking Go Live fails in front of the judges. The rest of the platform is genuinely offline; this one feature is not.

Even when a live feed is capturing correctly, the in-page preview can show "preview unsupported" — the player only renders .m3u8 natively, so an RTSP or YouTube URL is still being indexed on the backend but shows a warning triangle instead of video. If you improvise a non-HLS URL on stage it will look broken while actually working.
"Re-index" in the rail header, as previously reported: queues a full re-ingestion of all 16 videos on a CPU-only backend. Do not click it.
The camera rail is ordered by created_at DESC (CAM-16, 14, 15, 13, 12, 10, 11, 09…), as previously reported. Cosmetic.

questions.q: Is the citizen view just the staff view with things hidden by CSS?
questions.a: No. The case evidence list is filtered in the API — the same case returns 5 rows to an admin token and 1 row to the citizen token — and the staff-only endpoints answer 403 to this token, not 200-with-hidden-content. The nav difference is a consequence of the role, and the server would refuse the requests anyway.

questions.q: Why does the citizen see 6 cases when there are 10?
questions.a: Because case visibility to the complainant is an explicit per-case toggle an officer sets, not a default. Four cases have not been shared. That toggle also writes an audit row, so there is a record of who exposed what to whom and when.

questions.q: Can a citizen spam the investigating team with messages?
questions.a: No — the API caps it at one message per case per citizen and returns 403 'Citizens may send only one message per case' on the second attempt. It is enforced server-side, not by disabling a button.

questions.q: Where does the 4.17/5 satisfaction score on the command dashboard come from?
questions.a: From these accounts. When a case closes, the citizen gets a 'You may now rate your experience' notification and a star widget appears on the closed case. Six ratings have been given, averaging 4.17. The honest gap is that the rating is only ever shown back as a station-wide average — no case screen displays the rating that individual case received.

broken: The two newest complaints in the citizen's own list are QA artefacts: "QA probe scope test" (newest in the entire database, 2026-08-19 20:03:36 UTC) and "QA UPI OTP fraud 013203". If the demo script says 'let me triage the top complaint', the top complaint is a QA row.

Case #38 — the one closed case a citizen can open with a full verdict — was created by a QA agent's complaint-to-case conversion test, not by the seed. It looks completely realistic; the presenter should just not describe it as pre-existing station data.

It works, but do not scroll it and do not call it 'my complaints' in a way that invites counting.

The citizen advisory notification is the QA test broadcast — '[MEDIUM] QA test advisory — ignore: Pre-demo check of the broadcast pipeline. Deactivated immediately.' It is second from the top of the citizen bell.

questions.q: Is there a mobile app?
questions.a: No, and we would not build one yet — this is the same React app reflowing responsively, which means a constable at a scene sees exactly the same data as the control room with no second codebase to keep in sync and no app-store deployment path to negotiate with a police IT department. The trade-off is that it needs a browser and a connection.

questions.q: Why are the bottom tab icons unlabelled?
questions.a: A bug, and a small one: the bottom bar renders a property that does not exist on the nav item, so it prints nothing, while the desktop nav correctly resolves the same item through the translation catalogue. The labels exist in all three languages already. It is a one-word change that needs a frontend rebuild, which we are not doing the night before a demo.

broken: MOBILE BOTTOM TAB BAR HAS NO LABELS AT ALL — nine icon-only buttons on every screen, at every viewport below the md breakpoint. The cause is one word in frontend/src/App.jsx — the bottom bar renders {m.label} where the nav items carry labelKey and the desktop nav renders {t(m.labelKey)}. It is a one-word fix but it requires a frontend rebuild, so I did not apply it. Practical impact: if the presenter shrinks the window on stage to show the field view, the navigation loses all its text. Either show mobile deliberately and own it, or do not resize the window below ~768px during the demo.
The mobile bug is completely silent — zero console errors, zero API errors — which is exactly why five agents of desktop testing did not surface it.

Only the dashboard was exercised deeply at mobile size; the heavier screens (City Map with Leaflet, VisionScan result grids) were not measured for overflow at 390px, so do not promise that every module is phone-perfect.

headline.what: Emergency lockdown: "When active, only administrators can operate the platform — every other request is rejected (HTTP 423)." It has an inline two-step confirm before it can be enabled.
headline.why_impressive: A named HTTP status for a policy state, with a guard in front of it. It is the right answer to "what do you do during a breach" and the confirm step is evidence that someone thought about the operator, not just the feature.

headline.why_impressive: That is the nginx container's address, not any browser's. It is a one-glance proof of why the rate limiter treats all clients as one, and it turns a weakness into a technically literate observation the presenter volunteers first.
headline.exact_steps: Admin → security → "Recent login attempts". Point at the IP column.

headline.what: The data tab's four exports each state their own integrity property: "WAL-safe SQLite snapshot of the entire platform database", and "Every download is recorded in the audit log."

questions.q: What does emergency lockdown actually do?
questions.a: Every request from a non-admin account is rejected with HTTP 423 Locked until it is lifted. It is meant for a live incident or a suspected breach where you want the station's own administrators still able to operate while everything else is frozen. It requires a two-step confirm to enable, deliberately — it is a bigger hammer than any other control in the platform.

questions.q: Why does every login attempt show the same IP address?
questions.a: Because nginx proxies the API and the backend reads the connection's client address, which is the proxy container. nginx does set X-Real-IP but the backend is not consuming it. That is cosmetically wrong on this table, and functionally significant one layer down: the rate limiter keys on the same address, so every browser in the world shares one 120-requests-per-minute bucket. It is a small fix — trust the forwarded header — but it needs a backend restart, so it is not being changed tonight.

questions.q: Is the backup safe to take while the system is running?
questions.a: Yes — it is a WAL-safe SQLite snapshot rather than a file copy, so it does not capture a torn database mid-write. And the export itself is written to the audit log, so a handover is recorded rather than silent.

broken: "Sign out all my sessions" on the security tab has NO confirmation dialog — one click revokes every token on the admin account and drops the presenter back to the login screen. It is positioned directly beneath the lockdown card, which is the thing the presenter most wants to point at on that tab. This is the highest-consequence single-click mistake available in the product. If the security tab is shown at all, point with the mouse well away from it.

"Activate lockdown" does have a two-step inline confirm, so it cannot fire accidentally — but if it is ever confirmed, every officer and citizen request returns HTTP 423 and the entire multi-role story collapses. Only click it if you intend to immediately cancel.

There is no delete-user control in the UI to clean either up.

questions.q: What is the single biggest risk of something breaking live tomorrow?
questions.a: The shared rate limiter, and it is not close. I reproduced it: 150 sequential thumbnail requests trip HTTP 429 at request #124, in 2.38 seconds. /thumbnails/ falls into the same 120-requests-per-minute bucket as the API, and because nginx does not forward the client IP, EVERY browser shares ONE bucket — which you can see with your own eyes on Admin → security, where every login attempt logs IP 172.20.0.3. One idle tab already spends 66–74 of those 120 requests per minute on background polling. So a single ungrouped 60-card search grid is enough to break the demo, and the failure modes are ugly and silent: thumbnails render as black rectangles with bounding boxes floating on them, the entire Command Dashboard is replaced by one red 'Too many requests' box, the City Map hangs forever on 'Loading city intelligence…' with no error and no retry, CrimeGPT shows 'no open cases', and the Cases timeline shows 'No activity.' None of those look like rate limiting — they look like a broken product. The behavioural mitigations are: one tab only, grouping always ON, and if a screen goes blank, wait 30 seconds and let the poller heal it rather than clicking again.

questions.q: Is any headline item actually unimpressive or risky to show on stage?
questions.a: Four. (1) LIVE ALERTS. The headline is an architecture argument delivered over an empty screen. 'Zero false alarms on 417 frames' is a legitimate and honest claim, but you are asking judges to be impressed by a blank list — and the presenter cannot show a single detection. Either ingest a fire clip beforehand and accept that FEEDS goes 16→17, or move this screen to a 20-second architectural aside and do not build a beat around it. (2) SUSPECT FACE with grouping OFF. The report suggests toggling grouping off for a fuller 13-card grid; I measured the ungrouped tail and the weakest of the 13 scores 0.3247, barely over the 0.30 accept threshold. A grid whose last cards read 32% invites exactly the question you do not want. Keep grouping ON and open the gallery instead. (3) CASES BY SEVERITY on the dashboard. The report calls it a single 'High 9' bar that looks broken; it now has two bars (Critical 1, High 9), which is better but still the thinnest chart on a screen full of good ones. Skip it either way. (4) The PER-OBJECT 'red car' story, which is the strongest 20 seconds in VisionScan, has a trap directly attached: the frame-count badge promises 32 frames and the detail modal shows one image with no gallery. Tell the red-car story from the result grid, and tell the gallery story from a YOLO chip or the face search.

questions.q: Are any claims in the report implausible or contradictory?
questions.a: None were fabricated — I spot-checked the ones I doubted most and every single one held: the 24-vs-38 scoping inflation, the 13 hits for 'elephant in a swimming pool', the 0.86 reference-image match, the 0.8428 face match on CAM-07 with zero cross-camera hits, the IT Act 66F cyber-terrorism landmine, and the ungated zone/line endpoints. Two things drifted rather than being wrong: the backtest numbers moved slightly (HR@10 0.7786 not 0.7818, PAI@10 2.336 not 2.345) as the synthetic window slid, and the dashboard KPIs moved again overnight. One claim is now conservative in your favour: text search measured 37–48 ms tonight, not the reported 80 ms median. The one contradiction I found is between the report and the live data, not between agents: the Complaints page tells you to triage 'the top of the list', and the top of the list is now a QA test complaint.
